claim: ArtFlow's 'content leak' means the target content image losing detail when stylization is applied again and again. It is target-content degradation, not leakage of style-reference objects or layout into the output.
experiment: Iterated stylization: the stylized output is fed back as the new content image with the same style image, for 20 rounds, using AdaIN, WCT and Avatar-Net. Rounds 1 and 20 are shown.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 1): by round 20 the content details are hard to recognize for all three baselines.
direct_conclusion: Baseline encoder-decoder UST pipelines do not preserve target-content detail under repeated application. The paper names this 'Content Leak'. It is a target-content loss phenomenon that builds up over rounds.
author_hypothesis: Single-pass stylization also loses content information. The authors use repeated rounds as a proxy because content is hard to measure directly in a stylized image.
confounders: Repeated rounds amplify small per-pass errors, so this is an amplification proxy rather than a single-pass measurement. Examples are selected. The terminology clashes with diffusion-era 'content leakage' (reference semantics appearing in output), so the two must not be merged in a survey.
anchor: For a style transfer algorithm, Content Leak occurs because the stylization results lose some content information.

claim: With the transfer module held fixed, replacing the lossy, style-biased VGG auto-encoder with a lossless reversible network removes the 20-round content degradation for AdaIN/WCT and reduces it for the patch-swap Avatar-Net module.
experiment: Same iterated-stylization protocol (20 rounds). Compared: vanilla AdaIN, WCT, Avatar-Net and Self-Contained [9] vs ArtFlow+AdaIN, ArtFlow+WCT, ArtFlow+Avatar-Net (same transfer module, PFN in place of VGG encoder/decoder).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 10; more in Figs. 22-23). Authors: content leak 'disappears completely' for AdaIN/WCT with PFN and is 'significantly alleviated' for Avatar-Net.
direct_conclusion: On the shown examples, how features are recovered to pixels (lossless inversion vs learned decoder) controls how much target content is lost over repeated rounds. A biased transfer module such as patch replacement still causes some loss.
author_hypothesis: Content leak has three causes: decoder reconstruction error, biased decoder training (style loss in the decoder objective), and a biased transfer module (irreversible patch swap).
confounders: No per-round quantitative metric. The PFN is also trained with the style loss, so it differs from the VGG baseline in more than just reversibility. Examples are hand-picked.
anchor: when we replace the VGG19 based auto-encoder with the proposed PFN in AdaIN/WCT, the Content Leak disappears completely

claim: In a single pass, ArtFlow raises content-preservation scores without raising the Gram (style) loss relative to its own transfer module. Across methods, though, better content scores often go with weaker stylization (an operating-point confound).
experiment: MS-COCO content / WikiArt style. SSIM and VGG content loss to the content image; Gram-matrix MSE to the style image; runtime at 512x512. Compared with StyleSwap, AdaIN, WCT, LinearWCT, OptimalWCT, Avatar-Net and Self-Contained.
measured_outcome: Table 1 (SSIM / content loss / Gram loss): ArtFlow+AdaIN 0.45 / 2.58 / 0.00098 vs AdaIN 0.29 / 3.10 / 0.00127; ArtFlow+WCT 0.47 / 2.80 / 0.00078 vs WCT 0.27 / 3.35 / 0.00074; StyleSwap 0.44 / 2.22 / 0.00482; OptimalWCT 0.21 / 4.33 / 0.00035.
direct_conclusion: Relative to the same transfer module, PFN improves the SSIM and content-loss proxies at similar or lower Gram loss. StyleSwap (best content loss, worst Gram loss) and OptimalWCT (lowest Gram loss, lowest SSIM) show that content scores alone can reflect style dilution.
author_hypothesis: Higher SSIM shows that content leak is avoided, and comparable Gram loss shows stylization ability is not hurt.
confounders: SSIM and VGG content loss are proxies, and SSIM penalizes any texture change. Gram loss is a narrow style proxy. No reference-semantics leakage metric exists or applies, since the method uses global statistics.
anchor: ArtFlow achieves the highest SSIM score, which indicates that the proposed methods have a stronger ability to preserve

claim: An AdaIN decoder trained with a style loss reconstructs imperfectly by design. When applied repeatedly, it adds 'artistic' patterns, i.e. training-style priors intrude into the reconstructed content.
experiment: AdaIN decoder trained with content+style loss vs content loss only (loss curves). Separately, repeated encode-decode with the AdaIN auto-encoder, with no style transfer.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only. Fig. 3: converged content loss is visibly lower without the style loss (no numbers given). Fig. 4: odd artistic patterns appear as rounds increase (the text says 50 rounds; the figure shows rounds 1/20/40).
direct_conclusion: The learned decoder is a source of target-content distortion and of style bias that does not come from the current reference.
author_hypothesis: The AdaIN auto-encoder may memorize training styles and lean toward them at inference.
confounders: Loss curves are shown without numeric values. The round count differs between text and figure. Only one decoder is analyzed.
anchor: the auto-encoder of AdaIN is biased towards rendering more artistic effects, which causes Content Leak

claim: The 'unbiasedness' of AdaIN/WCT is a feature-space property under a bilinear content-times-style factorization. It defines style as global statistics and says nothing about leakage of reference semantics.
experiment: Proofs (Appendix B-C) that AdaIN and WCT satisfy C(fcs)=C(fc), S(fcs)=S(fs) under the bilinear definition. Fig. 7 plots content/style reconstruction error through PFN vs the VGG auto-encoder.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 7 curves; no table). The authors state PFN gives lossless content/style reconstruction with the AdaIN/WCT modules.
direct_conclusion: Under PFN, AdaIN/WCT are exact factor-swap operators for the chosen statistic. Avatar-Net's patch decorator does not fit the model and is called biased.
confounders: The result holds only if 'style' is fully captured by mean/std or covariance. It does not test style-factor entanglement (colour vs texture) or reference-layout transfer.
anchor: Theorem 1 The adaptive instance normalization in AdaIN is an unbiased style transfer module.

claim: Feature flow plus learned mask reduces adjacent-frame stability error vs per-frame baselines across four styles, at 2.5-2.8x runtime cost.
experiment: MPI Sintel test set (23 short videos, GT flow and occlusion); 4 styles; Johnson [23] and StyleBank [9] per-frame baselines vs with proposed sub-networks; fixed vs fine-tuned flow sub-network. Metric e_stab = masked ||O_t - W(O_{t-1})||^2 with GT flow and mask, averaged over video.
direct_conclusion: Adjacent-frame warping error in traceable regions decreases relative to per-frame processing; the optimization method of Ruder et al. remains lower (0.0067 vs 0.0105 on Candy).
author_hypothesis: Remaining gap to Ruder et al. is because the network is trained for all videos while optimization is per video.
confounders: Error magnitude varies ~5x across styles (Scream vs Candy), so the metric depends strongly on style texture; no style-fidelity metric in Table 1; Table 1 garbled (column assignment inferred).
anchor: for all the four styles, our method obtains much lower stability error than the baseline

claim: Lower stability error co-occurs with lower sharpness: composing features nearer the output lowers e_stab but reduces PSI, so the metric can be won by blur/ghosting.
experiment: Muse-style (inferred from matching baseline 0.0199) Johnson network; flow/mask inserted at five layers r1(E), r1/2(E), r1/4(E), r1/2(D), r1(D); e_stab and Perceptual Sharpness Index (PSI).
direct_conclusion: The lowest-error configurations are blurrier; the authors choose r1/4(E) as a compromise, i.e. e_stab alone is not a sufficient criterion and requires a fidelity/sharpness control.
author_hypothesis: Composition near the output blends already amplified differences and introduces ghosting; near the input small inconsistencies are amplified.
confounders: PSI is a sharpness proxy, not a style-fidelity measure; one style; single dataset.
locator: Section 4.4 'Layer Choice for Feature Composition'; Table 3
anchor: the stability is improved from input to output layers, while the sharpness decreases

claim: Training correspondence is DeepFlow2 flow on Ice Age/YouTube videos (supervising FlowNetS feature flow); evaluation uses Sintel ground-truth flow and occlusion masks.
experiment: Training set: ten videos (~28,000 frames); approximated ground truth flow from DeepFlow2 backward flow; masks from forward-backward cross-check and motion-boundary gradients. Test: MPI Sintel with GT flow and occlusion.
measured_outcome: Coherence loss and flow loss use DeepFlow2-derived W^g and M^g; e_stab uses Sintel GT W^g and M^g.
direct_conclusion: Evaluation correspondence differs in source from training correspondence (estimated vs synthetic GT), though both are dense 2-frame flow with occlusion masking and the metric equals the coherence-loss form.
confounders: Metric is identical in form to the training coherence loss; inference-time flow is FlowNetS feature flow, a third correspondence source.
anchor: we use DeepFlow2 [41] to compute the bidirectional optical flow and use the backward flow as the ground-truth

claim: Long-term consistency is claimed via recurrent feature propagation but never measured; authors acknowledge accumulated flow errors cause blurriness over long periods.
experiment: No long-range or reappearance metric; qualitative Fig. 6 shows two-frame pairs (static, camera motion, object motion).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only; limitations paragraph states errors accumulate after long propagation.
direct_conclusion: Only adjacent-frame consistency is quantified; propagation design does not handle reappearance after occlusion (features revert to current-frame values).
author_hypothesis: Propagating short-term coherence approximates long-term coherence until tracks end.
anchor: after propagation over a long period, small flow errors may accumulate, causing blurriness

claim: Temporal modules trained with a per-style network are not portable to other styles, but those trained with a multi-style StyleBank network transfer to new styles without retraining.
experiment: Cross combination: style sub-network of style A with flow/mask sub-networks trained for style B; e_stab on Sintel.
measured_outcome: Table 2, with [23]: Scream+Scream 0.0034; Scream+Candy 0.0042; Candy+Scream 0.0137; Candy+Candy 0.0105. With [9]: Scream+Scream 0.0031; Scream+multiple 0.0032; Candy+Candy 0.0121; Candy+multiple 0.0123.
direct_conclusion: Portability of the temporal asset depends on how the style network was trained: per-style coupling degrades stability (e.g. 0.0105 to 0.0137), multi-style training yields style-independent modules.
author_hypothesis: Sub-networks learned with a multiple-style-per-net can be independent of styles.
confounders: Only two styles; Table 2 [9] values (0.0031, 0.0121) differ from Table 1 [9]+Ours (0.0030, 0.0131), unexplained.
anchor: it is hard to preserve the original stability when our sub-networks trained on one style are applied to another

claim: Training without the auxiliary content adapter makes outputs adopt reference content semantics (e.g. the Mona Lisa face). So leakage depends on how content is routed during training, not only on the style representation.
experiment: Ablation grid (Fig. 7) of full model (with/without finetune), w/o ACA, w/o Explicit Adaptation, style encoder only. 3 example rows with prompts like 'A robot', 'A house covered with ice and snow'.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only. The authors report that without ACA the outputs are dominated by reference content features such as the Mona Lisa face.
direct_conclusion: In the shown examples, removing ACA from training brings back reference-content leakage even though the style representation is built from global VGG statistics.
author_hypothesis: ACA supplies content cues during training so that the style encoder and Explicit Adaptation learn 'pure' style instead of content semantics.
confounders: No leakage metric and no quantitative ablation table. Few examples. Whether the w/o-ACA model was retrained with identical schedules is not stated.
anchor: In its absence, the model inappropriately adopts content semantics.

claim: ACA works through a train/inference asymmetry. Fed with the reference at inference, it re-injects the reference's content structure. Dropping it at inference removes that structure while keeping style.
experiment: Appendix C.1: samples generated without vs with ACA active during denoising (Fig. 10), prompts 'A village', 'A flamingo'.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 10). With ACA during denoising, the reference content structures appear; omitting ACA removes them.
direct_conclusion: ACA absorbs the reference's coarse layout during training. At inference, leakage is controlled by removing that pathway, not by any test-time filtering of the style tokens.
author_hypothesis: During training, ACA and the prompt provide structure and semantics, so the style path does not need to encode them.
confounders: Qualitative, 2 examples. Training-time ACA uses the training image itself (reconstruction-style training), so the effect depends on ACA strength (deepest block, first 20% of steps, colour augmentation) chosen by hand.
anchor: by omitting ACA during inference, we can effectively remove these content structures while retaining the style representation

claim: The authors state that conditioning on global VGG mean/std statistics, which have no explicit spatial structure, can still transfer reference content patterns such as faces, through dataset-level overfitting.
experiment: Motivation for the ACA design. ACA is restricted to the deepest input block, the first 20% of denoising steps, and colour-augmented inputs (jitter, greyscale, inversion, polarization) so that it cannot carry palette.
measured_outcome: no direct measurement; the failure is asserted, and Fig. 7 (w/o ACA) is the closest evidence.
direct_conclusion: Representation choice alone (non-spatial statistics) does not, per the authors, guarantee freedom from reference-content leakage. A training-time routing component is needed.
author_hypothesis: Highly recurrent dataset patterns (e.g. human faces) lead the model to associate particular statistics with specific content.
confounders: The mechanism (statistics -> memorized content) is not tested directly. The ACA hyperparameters (20%, deepest block) are not ablated.
anchor: Even conditioning on VGG [27] statistics features without content structure, due to certain highly recurrent patterns in the dataset
review_note: Main reader: counterexample to the round-3 representation-and-binding-only account; supports acquisition as a third leakage source (F2.2).

claim: CLIP style similarity rewards methods that follow the reference closely at the cost of the prompt. Per-style finetuning raises style score and lowers text score, so text vs style scores show a trade-off, not a leakage measurement.
experiment: 35 prompts x 10 single-reference styles and 10 multi-reference style sets (700 pairs). CLIP text similarity, CLIP style similarity, aesthetics score. Baselines: CAST, StyTr2, T2I-Style-Adapter, InST, FreeDoM (single); TI, LoRA (multi).
direct_conclusion: Finetuning moves ArtAdapter along a text-style trade-off (style +0.051, text -0.014). The highest style score belongs to the method with the lowest text score. Multi-reference scores are near parity with TI/LoRA.
author_hypothesis: T2I-Style-Adapter's low text score reflects discarding the textual context.
confounders: There is no direct leakage metric, and CLIP style similarity can be inflated by copying reference content. The finetuned and zero-shot variants are at different operating points. User study (Table 2) compares only TI/LoRA, multi-ref.
anchor: highlights our style similarity score of 0.707 and an aesthetics score of 5.601, surpassing the benchmarks

claim: The low/mid/high style tokens are not cleanly separated. The authors report that high-level embeddings pick up lower-level elements, which interferes with cross-reference style mixing. This is style-factor entanglement, and also relevant to F1 composition interference.
experiment: Style mixing: low/mid tokens from one reference and high tokens from another (Fig. 4). Limitation stated in the Conclusion. Alpha scaling (Fig. 11) varies style vs text balance.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 4, Fig. 11). Interference is reported in prose, not measured.
direct_conclusion: Hierarchical VGG-level tokens give only partial factor control. Mixing levels from different references is affected by leakage between levels.
author_hypothesis: Better disentanglement of hierarchical features would fix the mixing interference.
confounders: Not quantified. Mixing examples are selected.
locator: Sec. 3.5; Sec. 4.2; Sec. 5 (Conclusion); Appendix C.2, Fig. 11
anchor: style embeddings often inadvertently incorporate elements from lower levels, causing interference in the style mixing process

claim: Removing the two-step (content-first, frozen) style-LoRA training produces visible content leakage; leakage is attributed to joint optimisation and epsilon-prediction.
experiment: Ablation variants: Var A epsilon-prediction instead of x0; Var B no two-step style training; Var C x0-only content LoRA (Fig. 9, Fig. 14).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: In the shown examples, how the style LoRA is acquired (jointly vs after freezing a content LoRA) changes visible reference-content leakage.
author_hypothesis: Joint optimisation makes LoRAs learn shared features, and epsilon-prediction makes the style LoRA capture local content details.
confounders: No leakage metric; prompt also changes ('A [v]' vs style-specific prompt) together with training schedule.
locator: Section 4.2 'Disentangling Style and Content'; Section 5.4; Fig. 9; Appendix D Fig. 14
anchor: Removing the two-step training strategy for style LoRA leads to significant content leakage issues.

claim: Reported style metrics barely separate ConsisLoRA from B-LoRA; the leakage-reduction claim is not quantified and the authors only hypothesise B-LoRA's style score is leakage-inflated.
experiment: 400 content-style pairs (20 x 20); style alignment by DreamSim distance and CLIP; content alignment by DINO, DreamSim, CLIP; vs StyleAligned, StyleID, ZipLoRA (community implementation), B-LoRA.
measured_outcome: Style DS (lower better): StyleAlign 0.591, StyleID 0.653, ZipLoRA 0.646, B-LoRA 0.573, Ours 0.567. Style CLIP: 0.645, 0.638, 0.643, 0.654, 0.659 (same order). Content columns TABLE_TEXT_GARBLED in column order (the text states StyleID is best on content and Ours improves most over B-LoRA on DINO).
direct_conclusion: On style metrics ConsisLoRA and B-LoRA differ by 0.006 DS and 0.005 CLIP; improvement is mainly in content alignment.
author_hypothesis: B-LoRA's comparable CLIP style score 'may be inflated due to content leakage'.
confounders: No leakage-specific metric; CLIP/DreamSim style metrics may reward leaked content; inference guidance disabled in comparison; unofficial ZipLoRA.
anchor: this score may be inflated due to content leakage from the reference image

claim: Attention-map visualisation is offered as mechanism evidence that B-LoRA's style token attends to local details, linked by the authors to leakage and misalignment.
experiment: Attention maps for style token '[v]' (ConsisLoRA vs B-LoRA) on two prompts (Fig. 18); loss-vs-timestep curve for epsilon vs x0 prediction (Fig. 3).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 3 shows epsilon loss high at small t, x0 loss high at large t)
direct_conclusion: Different training targets yield different attention concentration in the shown examples.
author_hypothesis: epsilon-prediction emphasises low-level details at small timesteps and neglects high-level structure/style.
confounders: Two examples; causal link from attention locality to leakage not tested.
anchor: B-LoRA tends to focus more on certain local details compared to our method

claim: ConsisLoRA's per-style asset costs more acquisition than B-LoRA (style image needs a content LoRA first), and controllable inference requires four LoRAs and extra passes.
experiment: Implementation details and inference-guidance formulation (Eq. 5).
measured_outcome: Content image: 500 + 1000 steps; style image: 1500-step content LoRA then 1000-step style LoRA; 'approximately 12 minutes on a single 4090 GPU' for the entire training process.
direct_conclusion: Reuse of a style LoRA across contents needs no extra optimisation, but guidance-based strength control needs the decomposition of both images (theta_cc, theta_cs, theta_sc, theta_ss).
confounders: Whether 12 minutes covers one image or a content-style pair is ambiguous; no inference-time measurement.
anchor: The entire training process takes approximately 12 minutes on a single 4090 GPU.

claim: Merged independently trained LoRAs (ZipLoRA) are observed to lose style balance, and users strongly prefer ConsisLoRA over both merge-based and block-based baselines.
experiment: User study: 50 participants, 1,500 responses, pairwise vs each baseline; qualitative comparison (Fig. 5, Fig. 10).
measured_outcome: Prefer baseline / prefer ours: B-LoRA 24.3% / 75.7%; ZipLoRA 11.7% / 88.3%; StyleID 19.2% / 80.8%; StyleAligned 10.4% / 89.6%.
direct_conclusion: Combined content+style preference favours ConsisLoRA; ZipLoRA's merged outputs are qualitatively described as sometimes neglecting style.
author_hypothesis: Structural inconsistency of baselines stems from epsilon-prediction capturing broad concepts.
confounders: Community ZipLoRA implementation; single combined question; no interference metric for merging.
anchor: ZipLoRA struggles to balance the merged content and style LoRAs, sometimes neglecting the style

claim: Style factors are carried by different mechanisms: removing initial-latent AdaIN sharply worsens colour transfer while improving LPIPS; removing K/V injection worsens style FID greatly. Colour and texture are bound through different loci.
experiment: 800 stylized images (20 MS-COCO contents x 40 WikiArt styles); configurations: A default (gamma=0.75), A* (gamma=0.6), B -style injection, C -attention scaling, D -initial latent AdaIN; metrics ArtFID, FID (stylized vs style images), LPIPS (vs content), and Histogram loss (HistoGAN RGB-uv Hellinger distance to style image, supplementary).
direct_conclusion: Initial-latent statistics mainly control colour tone (histogram loss 0.2804 -> 0.5235 without it), and their removal lowers LPIPS to 0.390, i.e. the colour component counts as 'content change' under LPIPS; K/V injection is the main carrier of style per FID.
author_hypothesis: Statistics of the initial noise largely affect colour and brightness; SA features have less effect on colour tone (Fig. 5).
confounders: LPIPS is texture/colour-sensitive (authors acknowledge), so LPIPS changes conflate colour transfer with structural distortion; whether C was run at gamma=0.75 or 0.6 is unclear (text compares A* vs C); single sample of 800 pairs.
anchor: even with injecting the query, key, and value of styles, the resulting images still preserve the color tone

claim: Query-preservation ratio gamma is a single knob trading target-content preservation against style strength; the paper reports a continuous LPIPS-FID curve rather than a leakage measure.
experiment: gamma swept over [0.3, 1.0] in steps of 0.1 on the 800-image set; FID (style) vs LPIPS (content) plotted against baselines; tau swept 1.0-1.5.
measured_outcome: Fig. 10 curves (exact per-point values not given in text; TABLE_TEXT_GARBLED for plot labels). Text: lower gamma reflects style strongly while losing content; tau increase lowers both FID and LPIPS with diminishing gains.
direct_conclusion: Content distortion and style strength move together along gamma; authors claim their curve dominates baselines at matched LPIPS or FID.
author_hypothesis: Interpolated query stays in-distribution near content (t-SNE and NN distances, supplementary).
confounders: FID to the style image set is a distributional proxy that would also reward copying reference content; only 40 styles; operating point chosen by authors.
anchor: the lower γ highly reflects the style while losing the content of the given image, and vice versa

claim: Self-attention K/V substitution reduces magnitude of attention logits (blurred maps); temperature scaling restores sharpness and reduces both FID and LPIPS, a binding-level fix for a failure that is neither leakage nor content loss per se.
experiment: Std of pre-softmax self-attention map with vs without style injection over timesteps (Fig. 4); tau sweep (Fig. 10b); ablation C (Table 3).
measured_outcome: Fig. 4: style injection lowers attention-map std across timesteps; average ratio used to set tau=1.5. Table 3: C (-attn scaling) ArtFID 29.02, FID 17.81, LPIPS 0.542 vs A* 27.97 / 17.21 / 0.535.
direct_conclusion: Cross-image K substitution changes attention statistics; temperature rescaling slightly improves both metrics at the tested setting.
author_hypothesis: Unrelated style/content patches yield low similarities, making attention overly smooth and outputs unsharp.
confounders: Small metric differences; A* vs C operating point unclear.
anchor: we validate that this style injection tends to lower the standard deviation of the attention map over the entire timesteps

claim: Target-content distortion is measured with a style-insensitive structural metric (CFSD) and LPIPS-gray; reference-content leakage is never measured, and the authors argue similarity-based K/V matching transfers local textures rather than reference objects.
experiment: CFSD = mean KL divergence between softmax-normalised VGG19 conv3 patch-similarity maps of content and stylized images; compared against 12 baselines on 800 images; LPIPS-gray and histogram loss on a second disjoint set (Table 5).
measured_outcome: Table 1 CFSD: Ours 0.2281; AesPA-Net 0.2464; AdaAttN 0.2862; DiffStyle 0.2819; InST 0.6759 (others in table). Ours ArtFID 28.801, FID 18.131, LPIPS 0.5055. Table 5 (new set): Ours ArtFID 30.38, FID 18.87, LPIPS 0.528, LPIPS-Gray 0.417, Histogram-loss 0.303.
direct_conclusion: StyleID preserves target spatial correlation better than baselines on this protocol; no measurement addresses whether style-image objects/layout appear in outputs.
author_hypothesis: Query-key similarity matches content patches to style patches with similar local texture (e.g. edges), so similar content patches receive similar style (Fig. 2).
confounders: Fig. 2 evidence is a PCA/similarity visualisation on selected examples; FID-to-style may reward leakage; baselines run with recommended configs, not strength-matched except in Fig. 10.
locator: Section 5.2; Section 5.3; Table 1; Supplementary Table 5; Fig. 2
anchor: Content Feature Structural Distance (CFSD) which is a distance measure that only considers the spatial correlation between image patches

claim: Starting from the style latent instead of content latent makes output structure follow the style image (reference layout leakage via initial noise); AdaIN on channel statistics is the authors' fix.
experiment: Described observation motivating initial latent AdaIN; no figure or metric of the style-latent variant is reported.
measured_outcome: no measurement of the failure
direct_conclusion: The paper asserts that full style-latent initialisation transfers reference structure; only the mitigation is evaluated (Table 3/4).
author_hypothesis: Tone information is tied to channel statistics of the initial latent while structure is tied to spatial content of the latent.
anchor: the structural information of synthesized results also follows the style image and loses the structure of the content

claim: Training-free attention injection removes per-style optimisation but nothing is reusable across pairs: each content and style must be inverted; reported per-pair cost 12.4 s vs 355.9-816.9 s for diffusion baselines.
experiment: Inference time for one content-style pair on a single TITAN RTX GPU vs DiffuseIT, InST, DiffStyle.
measured_outcome: Table 2: DiffuseIT 792.8 s; InST 816.9 s; DiffStyle 355.9 s; Ours 12.4 s (8.2 s DDIM inversions + 4.2 s sampling).
direct_conclusion: Per-pair cost is dominated by inversion; InST's cost includes per-style textual inversion optimisation.
author_hypothesis: Fewer inversion steps suffice because features cached during inversion reduce the need for perfect inversion.
confounders: Baselines differ in backbone and resolution; no amortised comparison (e.g. one style applied to many contents) where InST's learned embedding could be reused.
anchor: Our method requires a total of 12.4 seconds, with 8.2 seconds for DDIM inversions and 4.2 seconds for sampling costs

claim: Temporal coherence is argued by a linearity bound (output feature change bounded by |K| times input feature change), not enforced by any correspondence; the bound ignores normalization and the decoder.
experiment: Coherence analysis: assumes ||f_c^m - W f_c^n|| < delta for coherent input; derives ||K f_c^m - W K f_c^n|| = |K| ||f_c^m - W f_c^n|| < |K| delta.
measured_outcome: Derivation only (eq. 7-10). The decoder's effect is checked only qualitatively via a relu3_1 vs relu4_1 depth ablation (Fig. 12).
direct_conclusion: The argument shows feature-level Lipschitz-type transfer of input coherence if K is frame-independent and commutes with warping; it does not address occlusion, normalization of f_c (applied before MCC), or the nonlinear decoder, and gives no guarantee about magnitude of |K|.
author_hypothesis: MCCNet migrates the coherence of input frame features to stylized features without additional temporal constraints, and this survives decoding.
confounders: Input features are normalized per frame before MCC (content-dependent statistics); the bound scales with |K|, which grows with style energy.
locator: Section 3.2 eq. (7)-(10); Section 3.3; Section 4.4 'Network depth'; Fig. 12
anchor: our network can migrate the coherence of the input video frame features to the stylized frame features without additional temporal constraints

claim: Quantitative temporal metric is unwarped adjacent-frame difference with no occlusion handling; a static output would score best, and the method's error is about twice the input's.
experiment: 14 stylized clips per method; Diff_F(t) = ||F_t - F_{t-1}|| for adjacent frames; mean and variance over clips; methods: Ours, MAST, CompoundVST, Linear, AAMS, WCT, AdaIN, NST, plus inputs.
direct_conclusion: MCCNet has the lowest mean raw frame difference among compared methods, with Linear close (0.0314); all outputs differ more frame-to-frame than the inputs. Because no warping is applied, the metric mixes motion with flicker and rewards outputs that change less regardless of motion.
author_hypothesis: Differences closest to those of the input frames indicate coherence without damaging stylization.
confounders: No flow/warping or occlusion mask; no style-fidelity metric on the same clips; identity of the 14 clips/styles and source dataset not specified beyond Sintel figure; table garbled into fragments (column assignment inferred from count).
anchor: we define Dif f F (t) = ||Ft − Ft−1 || and calculate the mean (meanDif f ) and variance (varDif f )

claim: Illumination (noise-robustness) loss slightly lowers adjacent-frame difference; it targets intensity perturbation, not motion correspondence.
experiment: Model trained without illumination loss vs full model; heat maps of differences between two video frames (Fig. 10) and mean frame difference.
measured_outcome: Without illumination loss mean difference 0.0317 (text); full model 0.0297 (Table 2).
direct_conclusion: Training for invariance to additive Gaussian noise reduces raw frame difference modestly; no evidence about consistency under motion or occlusion.
author_hypothesis: Gaussian noise simulates illumination variation; illumination loss makes the model robust to complex lighting.
confounders: Gaussian noise is a weak proxy for illumination change; single scalar; unclear whether same clips.
anchor: frames increase, with the mean value being 0.0317. With illumination loss

claim: Joint style-plus-stability judgement exists only as a pairwise video user study; frame-level stylization strength vs stability is not reported together quantitatively.
experiment: Pairwise video user study: input clip + style image, Ours vs random competitor, choose most satisfying considering stylized effect and stability; 700 votes from 50 participants.
measured_outcome: Fig. 7(b) — percentages not extractable from text (TABLE_TEXT_GARBLED / figure only).
direct_conclusion: A combined preference was collected, but stability and style strength are not separated, so it cannot show the method avoids winning by weaker stylization.
author_hypothesis: Our method can achieve the best video stylization effect.
confounders: CompoundVST excluded from user study; SANet and DFP excluded from video comparison.
anchor: we asked the participants which stylized video clip is the most satisfying by considering

claim: Qualitative comparisons attribute reference-patch copying to attention-based SANet and style dilution to Linear; removing multi-channel correlation causes dilution and retained content colour.
experiment: Image comparisons vs SANet, Linear, AdaIN, WCT, AAMS, DFP, MAST, NST (Fig. 5); ablation channel-wise vs multi-channel correlation (Fig. 9); content/style classification accuracy (Fig. 6, values not in text).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (classification accuracies in Fig. 6 not extractable).
direct_conclusion: Failure types (reference patch transfer, dilution, colour retention) are named per method from selected examples only; no leakage metric.
author_hypothesis: Correlation-based rearrangement fits style patterns to content structure.
confounders: Cherry-picked examples; operating points not matched.
anchor: Some style image patches are transferred into the content image directly (the first row) by SANet

claim: Only ~3K of ~1.6M parameters (~0.2%) are style-specific; style-specific parameters grow O(N x L) with the number of styles.
experiment: Parameter count of the CIN architecture (Appendix Table 1).
measured_outcome: roughly 1.6M parameters total, around 3K (0.2%) per style
direct_conclusion: Per-style storage/transmission is small, but the style vector is only meaningful together with the specific shared network (non-portable across checkpoints).
author_hypothesis: Small per-style footprint enables storing/transmitting new styles to mobile devices.
confounders: Mobile deployment is not tested.
anchor: only around 3K (or 0.2%) of which specify individual artistic styles

claim: Folding 10 styles into one network slightly raises final content loss versus single-style networks, while style loss difference is insignificant.
experiment: 10 Monet paintings: 10-style CIN network vs 10 separately trained single-style networks; losses averaged over 32 random content batches (Fig 5).
measured_outcome: 10-style content loss 8.7 +/- 3.9% higher; style loss 8.9 +/- 16.5% lower (insignificant).
direct_conclusion: Sharing weights across stylistically similar styles costs a modest content-loss increase at equal per-network update count.
author_hypothesis: Comparison may be unfair since N single-style networks receive N times more total parameter updates.
confounders: Stylistically similar styles (all Monet); losses are proxies; the 32-style varied model is not quantitatively compared.
anchor: The 10-styles network’s content loss is around 8.7 ± 3.9% higher than its

claim: A new style still requires per-style optimization, though only of gamma/beta: 5,000 steps on frozen shared weights yields pastiches comparable to a 40,000-step from-scratch network.
experiment: Incremental addition of Monet's Plum Trees in Blossom to the 32-varied-style network vs training a single-style network from scratch; learning curves and pastiches (Fig 6).
measured_outcome: Fine-tuned 5,000 steps comparable to 40,000-step scratch model (visual); 5,000 scratch steps gives poor pastiche; curve values not readable from text.
direct_conclusion: Shared weights transfer to an unseen style but only after style-specific training; the model cannot stylize an unseen style at test time without optimization.
author_hypothesis: The network 'generalizes across painting styles'.
confounders: Single added style; Plum Trees appears in the separate 10-Monet set, so the style family may be close to training distribution; comparison is visual.
anchor: keep the trained weights fixed and learn a new set of γ and β parameters

claim: Convex combinations of learned gamma/beta give smooth style blends; style loss to each endpoint varies monotonically with the mixing weight.
experiment: Interpolation alpha in [0,1] between Bicentennial Print and Head of a Clown, style loss w.r.t. each painting for one source image; four-style convex combinations shown qualitatively (Fig 7, Fig 1b).
measured_outcome: Style losses vary monotonically as alpha moves 0 to 1 (plot; axis up to ~8.3e9, individual values not readable).
direct_conclusion: Composition within the trained style set is possible without retraining; the study shows no interference metric beyond monotonic loss on one pair.
author_hypothesis: The parameters form an embedding of styles.
confounders: One content image and one style pair quantified; only trained styles; no measure of whether blends are perceptually coherent vs overlaid.
anchor: Head of a Clown paintings, as we vary α from 0 to 1

claim: Block-separated B-LoRAs can be recombined across images without a per-pair optimisation; cost is one ~10-minute fit per image.
experiment: Implementation details plus mixing grids (Fig. 27, Fig. 28) combining Delta W^4 of row i with Delta W^5 of column j.
measured_outcome: 1000 optimisation steps, rank 64, ~10 minutes per image on a single A100; storage reduced by 70% relative to full LoRA (stated); mixing grids qualitative only.
direct_conclusion: Composition is by direct plugging of pre-trained blocks; no extra composition optimisation is needed by construction.
author_hypothesis: Runtime is comparable to StyleDrop/ZipLoRA (which also need LoRA training), and ZipLoRA is slower due to its extra merging phase.
confounders: No measured runtime comparison; recombination quality not measured across a controlled grid.
anchor: for 1000 optimization steps, requiring approximately 10 minutes per

claim: The style/content block assignment is specific to SDXL's block layout, so B-LoRA assets are backbone-bound; no other backbone is tested.
experiment: Prompt-injection analysis: inject p_hat into one of six intermediate SDXL blocks, measure CLIP similarity to p_hat over 400 content/style prompt pairs; block-pair LoRA reconstruction grid (Fig. 19-20).
measured_outcome: Blocks W^2 and W^4 dominate content, W^5 dominates colour (no numeric scores printed); block-pair grid qualitative.
direct_conclusion: Separation is located in specific SDXL blocks, using colour as a CLIP-measurable proxy for style.
author_hypothesis: Style-content disentanglement is innate to SDXL's layers.
confounders: Colour as style proxy; analysis on generated (not real) images; per-block scores not reported.
anchor: In total, we examined 400 pairs of content and style prompts and averaged the scores of each layer.

claim: In LoRA-based baselines, the content asset's operating point (single vs multiple content images) trades style against content, indicating composition interference via content overfitting.
experiment: DINO ViT-B/8 cosine similarity of output to style and content references; 50 style-content pairs (23 objects, 25 styles); baselines (StyleDrop-on-SDXL, StyleAligned, unofficial ZipLoRA, DB-LoRA+ControlNet) with multiple vs single content images.
measured_outcome: TABLE_TEXT_GARBLED for Table 1 per-method values. Text: single-content setting gives 'a decrease in style consistency scores across all methods, accompanied by an increase in content preservation scores'. Supplementary Table 2 (single image, Style/Content): StyTr2 0.83/0.854, AdaAttn 0.818/0.828, SWAG 0.883/0.788, Ours 0.881/0.790.
direct_conclusion: With the DINO proxy, baseline content LoRAs that preserve content more strongly lower style similarity; B-LoRA does not dominate both axes (lower content score than StyTr2/AdaAttn in Supp. Table 2).
author_hypothesis: Lower object similarity of B-LoRA reflects baselines' content overfitting rather than worse content preservation.
confounders: Baselines re-implemented on SDXL (unofficial ZipLoRA); DINO conflates content and style; interpretation of higher content score as 'overfitting' is untested.
anchor: The results indicate a decrease in style consistency scores across all methods, accompanied by an increase in content preservation scores

claim: Implicit block separation leaves factor entanglement and leakage: object colour goes into the style block (identity loss) and background elements of the style image enter the style component.
experiment: Limitations figure (Fig. 9a-c) and mitigation figures (alpha 0.4-0.5 on Delta W^5, Fig. 17; centre cropping; block-specific prompt injection, Fig. 18).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Colour-identity coupling and background leakage persist under B-LoRA's block routing; mitigations are strength scaling and preprocessing.
author_hypothesis: Single-reference training makes the style component encompass background elements.
confounders: No frequency estimate; alpha scaling may simply dilute style.
anchor: our learned style component may encompass background elements rather than focusing solely on the central object

claim: User preference favours B-LoRA over leakage-prone or content-overfitting baselines, but leakage itself is only shown qualitatively.
experiment: User study: 30 random pairs (10 per baseline), 34 participants, 1020 answers, 'better transfers the style ... while preserving the content'.
measured_outcome: 94% prefer B-LoRA over StyleAligned, 91% over ZipLoRA, 88% over StyleDrop. StyleAligned leakage (two cats matching two people in the style image) shown qualitatively (Fig. 8).
direct_conclusion: Combined style+content preference favours B-LoRA; the study does not isolate leakage.
author_hypothesis: Attention-sharing (StyleAligned) and encoder-based methods lack style-content separation and leak structure.
confounders: Baselines re-implemented on SDXL (StyleDrop via StyleAligned's recipe; unofficial ZipLoRA); single combined question; small set.
anchor: with 94% of participants favoring our method over StyleAligned, 91% over ZipLoRA, and 88% over StyleDrop

claim: Output warping error e_stab rewards weak stylization: Huang et al., whose stylization the authors describe as weak, and the optimization method score lower error than ReCoNet.
experiment: 5 MPI Sintel scenes, single style Candy, 640x360; compared Chen et al., ReCoNet, Huang et al., Ruder et al. Metric e_stab = sqrt of mean over frames of occlusion-masked ||O_t - W_t(O_{t-1})||^2 / D with GT flow.
direct_conclusion: Among real-time methods, ReCoNet has lower e_stab than Chen et al. but higher than Huang et al.; the authors themselves argue the lower error of Huang et al. coincides with weaker strokes/textures, i.e. the metric alone cannot separate consistency from stylization strength.
author_hypothesis: Huang et al.'s low error stems from a low perceptual-to-temporal loss ratio that weakens style; ReCoNet's new losses allow a higher ratio.
confounders: Only one style (Candy); no quantitative style-fidelity metric reported jointly; different training data/loss weights across compared models; style strength judged qualitatively/user study only.
anchor: Although our temporal error is higher than Huang et al [17]'s model, our model is capable of capturing strokes

claim: Training and evaluation use the same kind of correspondence (ground-truth synthetic optical flow and occlusion masks), from different datasets; no estimated flow at test.
experiment: Training on Monkaa and FlyingThings3D (Scene Flow) with their GT flow; occlusion masks via Sundaram et al.; evaluation on MPI Sintel GT flow/occlusion; FlowNet2 used only for the input-warping-error histogram analysis on Videvo videos.
measured_outcome: Losses use ground-truth forward optical flow W_t and ground-truth forward occlusion mask M_t; e_stab uses the same variables on Sintel.
direct_conclusion: The metric measures exactly the masked flow-warped output equality that the output-level loss (minus its luminance term) optimizes, with GT flow of the same type; the evaluation is therefore well matched to the training signal and adjacent-frame only.
author_hypothesis: Using GT flow only in training avoids optical-flow prediction errors and speeds inference.
confounders: Synthetic-to-synthetic domain (animated) for both training and metric; real-world Videvo videos evaluated only via user study.
locator: Section 2 (last paragraph); Section 3.3 eq. (1),(2); Section 4.1; eq. (4)
anchor: our model does not estimate optical flows but involves ground-truth optical flows only in loss calculation in the training stage

claim: Feature-map-level temporal loss alone is weaker than output-level loss; combining both yields only a marginal average gain over output-only.
experiment: Candy style, 5 Sintel scenes; feature-map only vs output only vs both; e_stab.
measured_outcome: Average e_stab: Feature-map only 0.0975; Output only 0.0813; Both 0.0804. Per scene (Alley-2..Temple-2): Feature-map only 0.1028/0.1041/0.0752/0.1062/0.0991; Output only 0.0854/0.0840/0.0672/0.0868/0.0820; Both 0.0846/0.0819/0.0662/0.0862/0.0831 (Temple-2 slightly worse with both).
direct_conclusion: Output-level warping loss provides most of the measured reduction; feature-level benefit is about 0.0009 on average and shown for traceable objects qualitatively (Fig. 6).
author_hypothesis: Same object should have the same high-level features, improving consistency on traceable objects.
confounders: Single style; no variance or seeds; output-only average 0.0813 does not equal the arithmetic mean of its five printed values (0.0811), possibly frame-weighted.
anchor: while the feature-map-level temporal loss also improves temporal consistency on average

claim: Luminance-warping constraint lowers e_stab versus no constraint or an XYZ variant, motivated by brightness constancy failing even along GT flow.
experiment: Candy style, same Sintel scenes; approach 1 (relative luminance constraint on each RGB channel), 2 (XYZ with Y constraint), 3 (no luminance constraint). Motivation: histograms of input warping error |I_t - W_t(I_{t-1})| on Sintel and 50 Videvo videos (FlowNet2 flow).
measured_outcome: e_stab: approach 1 = 0.0804, approach 2 = 0.0957, approach 3 = 0.0911 (Fig. 7). Histograms qualitatively show nonzero warping error in RGB and XYZ channels (exact values TABLE_TEXT_GARBLED).
direct_conclusion: On this style and these scenes, modelling input luminance change along flow reduces the masked warping error of outputs.
author_hypothesis: Illumination effects violate brightness constancy so pure flow warping misjudges traceable pixels; chromaticity changes are ignored for lack of a guideline.
confounders: Single style; no style-fidelity numbers per variant ('pleasant perceptual styles... despite some variations in color').
anchor: adding a relative luminance warping constraint to all RGB channels can generate smoother color change

claim: User study separates style resemblance from temporal consistency: Huang et al. preferred on consistency, ReCoNet on style, showing a style-consistency trade-off.
experiment: 50 participants, 4 styles on 4 Videvo clips per comparison; Q1 style resemblance, Q2 temporal consistency, Q3 overall preference.
measured_outcome: Table 3 votes (Q1/Q2/Q3): ReCoNet 64/162/152 vs Chen 64/15/23 vs Same 72/23/25; ReCoNet 164/42/115 vs Huang 22/91/42 vs Same 14/67/43.
direct_conclusion: The only joint fidelity-consistency control is subjective; human raters judged Huang et al. more temporally consistent but much weaker in style.
confounders: Short-clip user study; votes aggregated over clips and styles; details in supplement not in this text.
anchor: our results are much better in perceptual styles and the overall feeling although our temporal consistency is slightly worse

claim: Style is bound to network weights; per-frame inference is cheap and flow-free, but each style requires full training.
experiment: Inference FPS on GTX 1080 Ti at 640x360 (Candy).
measured_outcome: ReCoNet 235.3 FPS vs Chen et al. 22.5, Huang et al. 216.8, Ruder et al. 0.8 (Table 2). Training: 30,000 steps, batch size 2 (no wall-clock reported).
direct_conclusion: Per-content cost is negligible once the per-style network exists; training cost per style is not quantified.
author_hypothesis: Feed-forward designs parallelize better than recurrent ones because frames need not wait for the previous frame.
confounders: FPS for other methods measured by authors on their hardware; implementations may differ.
anchor: feedforward models are easier to be accelerated with parallelism since the current iteration do not need to wait

claim: For a CLIP-encoder adapter (StyleCrafter retrained on StyleGallery), lowering the injection scale replaces content leakage with style dilution. Strength tuning does not separate the two.
experiment: StyleCrafter trained on StyleGallery, inference at lambda = 1.0 vs 0.5, compared to StyleShot (Fig. 10).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only. At lambda=1: 'significant content leakage'. At lambda=0.5: weakened style, some outputs look like real-world photos.
direct_conclusion: With a semantic CLIP-feature style representation, the only knob shown (scale) moves along a leakage-dilution axis, at least in the displayed examples.
author_hypothesis: A frozen CLIP encoder captures mainly semantics, so its style tokens bring content with them.
confounders: Few examples, no metric. Only two scale values. StyleShot's own scale sensitivity is not shown.
anchor: results in significant content leakage issue while setting the scale value λ = 0.5 diminished the style injection

claim: StyleShot tries to suppress spatial content in its representation (non-adjacent patches, no position embeddings), yet trains by reconstruction and explicitly counts layout as a style attribute it transfers.
experiment: Method/implementation description: each training image is both the U-Net target and the style reference. Captions are de-stylized (style words removed). Patch-scale dropping (Fig. 11) and baseline vs fine-tuning vs multi-scale (Fig. 13) are qualitative ablations.
measured_outcome: Fig. 11 / Fig. 13: qualitative figure only. Small patches alone carry mostly colour, and adding larger patches adds high-level style.
direct_conclusion: The representation is built to remove positional structure but keeps 'layout' as style (Fig. 1 caption, conclusion). The paper does not define when reference layout is style and when it is leakage.
author_hypothesis: High-level styles (3D, flat) are global, so they need larger patches. Dropping position embeddings removes spatial structure information.
confounders: There is no leakage metric to test whether dropping position embeddings reduces leakage. Patch partitioning keeps local object parts inside larger patches.
locator: Sec. 3.2; Sec. 4.4; Fig. 1; Figs. 11, 13; Appendix B.1
anchor: we drop the position embeddings to get rid of the spatial structure information in patches

claim: StyleShot uses a reconstruction objective (the reference equals the target), which DEADiff blames for leakage. It counters prompt-reference entanglement by removing style words from captions, which gives a small image-alignment gain.
experiment: Model trained with original captions (containing style descriptions) vs de-stylized captions, scored by CLIP image alignment on StyleBench.
measured_outcome: Table 6 (CLIP image): With Style 0.631; De-Style 0.640.
direct_conclusion: Removing style words from captions slightly raises CLIP image alignment to the reference. The effect is small, and the CLIP image metric does not tell style gain from leakage gain.
author_hypothesis: Style words in captions let the text path carry style, which keeps the image encoder from learning it.
confounders: There is a single metric, and it is leakage-sensitive. No text-alignment number for this ablation. The difference of 0.009 has no variance reported.
locator: Sec. 3.4 (De-stylization); Appendix B.1; Appendix B.5, Table 6
anchor: Then the image is sent to the U-Net as the target image and to the Style-Aware
review_note: Main reader: conflicts with DEADiff attribution of leakage to reconstruction training (F2.4).

claim: On StyleBench, the methods the authors flag for content leakage (StyleCrafter, StyleAligned) have the HIGHEST CLIP image-alignment scores. Humans prefer StyleShot for both style and text.
experiment: StyleBench: 73 styles, 490 reference images, 20 prompts, 40 content images. Text-driven comparison with StyleCrafter, DEADiff, StyleDrop (unofficial), InST, StyleAligned. Human study: 30 tasks, 1320 responses, choose best style match and best text match. CLIP text and image scores.
measured_outcome: Table 1 human (text / image %): StyleCrafter 9.7 / 14.3; DEADiff 19.3 / 8.0; StyleDrop 6.0 / 4.0; InST 12.7 / 6.3; StyleAligned 8.0 / 17.3; StyleShot 44.3 / 50.0. CLIP (text / image): StyleCrafter 0.202 / 0.706; DEADiff 0.232 / 0.597; StyleDrop 0.220 / 0.621; InST 0.204 / 0.623; StyleAligned 0.213 / 0.680; StyleShot 0.219 / 0.640.
direct_conclusion: CLIP image similarity to the reference ranks the leakage-prone methods first, so it cannot serve as a style-fidelity measure where leakage is present. DEADiff has the highest CLIP text score but low human style preference.
author_hypothesis: CLIP scores are not ideal for style transfer evaluation (citing StyleDrop and StyleCrafter).
confounders: Leakage is only qualitative (Appendix B.3, Fig. 19, rows 4-9). Human study is forced-choice best-of-6 on 30 tasks. StyleDrop is an unofficial implementation.
locator: Sec. 4.1; Sec. 4.3; Table 1; Appendix A; Appendix B.2-B.3; Fig. 19
anchor: we also observe the issue of content leakage in lines 4-6 and 7-9, leading to a failure

claim: Edge maps (Canny, HED) used as target-content input still carry the content image's high-level style. Thresholded and dilated HED contours give stronger stylization. Target-structure preservation is claimed, not measured.
experiment: Pretrained ControlNet conditioned on Canny vs HED vs their contour input, combined with the style encoder. Then their content-fusion encoder trained with the style encoder (Fig. 14). Image-driven CLIP image scores vs AdaAttN, EFDM, StyTR-2, CAST, InST, StyleID.
measured_outcome: Fig. 5 / Fig. 14: qualitative figure only. Table 2 (CLIP image): AdaAttN 0.569; EFDM 0.561; StyTR-2 0.586; CAST 0.575; InST 0.569; StyleID 0.604; StyleShot 0.660. No content-preservation metric reported.
direct_conclusion: How the target content is represented (raw features vs edges vs coarse contours) controls how much of the content image's own style survives. Stronger de-stylization raises style strength, but target-structure fidelity is never quantified.
author_hypothesis: Content features are coupled with style, so manipulating them keeps the content's original style. Contour pre-decoupling solves this.
confounders: There is no SSIM/LPIPS/structure metric, so target distortion is unknown. CLIP image alignment again rewards closeness to the reference. Thresholding and dilation discard fine content detail.
locator: Sec. 3.3; Sec. 4.2; Sec. 4.4; Fig. 5; Fig. 14; Table 2
anchor: some high-level styles are still implicitly present in the edge details

claim: Optimization-based acquisition requires no style-specific training; style is a statistic computed from one exemplar, but the output is produced by per-pair iterative optimization.
experiment: Method description; no runtime measurement in this paper.
measured_outcome: No speed, iteration count, or hardware reported in this paper.
direct_conclusion: Per-style state = Gram matrices of one image; per-content cost = full optimization from white noise. Cost figures for this method must be taken from later papers (e.g., Johnson Table 1).
confounders: Paper is a short arXiv note; no convergence criterion or iteration count is given.
anchor: we use gradient descent from a white noise image to find another image that matches the style representation

claim: Gram-based style representation discards global arrangement; style reconstructions are texturised versions of the reference, whose local structure grows with layer depth.
experiment: Style reconstructions from Gram matrices on increasing layer subsets (conv1_1 to conv1_1..conv5_1), one image per subset (Fig 1).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: The representation retains colour and localized structure but not scene layout, so wholesale copying of reference layout is not expected from this carrier; local motifs can still be transferred at larger scale when deeper layers are included.
author_hypothesis: Increasing local structure size is explained by increasing receptive field size and feature complexity.
confounders: Single illustrative images; no leakage metric; reference object semantics at local scale are not separated from 'style'.
anchor: which captures its texture information but not the global arrangement

claim: Content/style balance is a single scalar trade-off; strong style emphasis yields a texturised artwork with little photo content (target-content distortion), strong content emphasis weakens style (dilution).
experiment: Grid over alpha/beta ratios (columns) x style layer subsets (rows) for one content photo and one style (Kandinsky Composition VII), Fig 3.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only; ratios used for Fig 2 were 1e-3 (B,C,D) or 1e-4 (E,F)
direct_conclusion: Target-content distortion and style dilution are two ends of one weighting knob for a given pair; weighting must be tuned per pair (different ratios used across Fig 2 panels).
author_hypothesis: Content and style cannot be completely disentangled; usually no image perfectly matches both constraints.
confounders: One style/content pair; per-pair tuned ratios; visually judged.
anchor: A strong emphasis on style will result in images that match the appearance of the artwork

claim: Warp error (RAFT flow of the input video) ranks Rerender-a-Video best, below even the unedited LDM reconstruction; authors argue warp error misses long-range inconsistencies and rely on a user study.
experiment: 61 text-video pairs (DAVIS + Internet, 40-200 frames); warp error using RAFT flow of the original video; 2AFC user study (2000-3000 judgments per baseline) on temporal consistency and motion preservation; CLIP text similarity.
measured_outcome: Warp-err x10^-3: LDM recon 2.0, PnP 11.3, Text2Video-Zero 12.5, Tune-a-Video 30.0, Fate-Zero 6.9, Rerender-a-Video 1.8, Ours 3.0. CLIP: LDM recon 0.23, PnP 0.33, Ours 0.33, others 0.31-0.33. User preference for ours vs Rerender 71%.
direct_conclusion: A flow-based method optimised for warp error wins on warp error; TokenFlow is second among editors. The fidelity metric (CLIP) barely separates methods (per-frame PnP also 0.33).
author_hypothesis: Optical-flow reliance creates long-range inconsistencies not reflected in warp error.
confounders: Metric correspondence (RAFT) resembles Rerender's own optimisation target; horizon of warp error and occlusion masking unstated; Gen-1 excluded from warp error due to frame-count mismatch.
anchor: optimizes for the warping error and uses optical flow to propagate the edit

claim: Replacing correspondence-based token propagation with extended attention to keyframes roughly doubles warp error at equal CLIP score, indicating extended attention alone gives weaker fine-grained temporal consistency.
experiment: Ablation on the same 61 pairs: TokenFlow vs 'w joint attention' (extended attention between each frame and keyframes) vs fixed evenly spaced keyframes.
measured_outcome: Warp-err x10^-3: w joint attention 5.9, w/o random keyframes 3.7, Ours 3.0; CLIP 0.33 for all three; user preference for ours vs joint attention 90%.
direct_conclusion: Under RAFT warp error, NN-field feature propagation is more consistent than extended attention at matched CLIP fidelity.
author_hypothesis: Extended attention preserves motion only implicitly.
confounders: Warp error is computed along the input video's motion, which TokenFlow explicitly copies by construction; CLIP is a coarse fidelity control.
anchor: solely relying on the extension of self-attention to multiple frames is insufficient for achieving fine-grained

claim: Correspondences come from the input video, so the method cannot handle structure-changing edits and enforces meaningless correspondences when the image editor fails to preserve structure.
experiment: Stated limitations with failure example (Fig. 7, 'A tractor').
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Input-correspondence propagation constrains consistency only where output structure matches input structure.
anchor: When the image-editing technique fails to preserve the structure, our method enforces correspondences that are meaningless in the edited frames

claim: Correspondence accuracy is evaluated only indirectly by feature-space reconstruction; RGB correspondence accuracy is explicitly not evaluated.
experiment: Reconstruct videos with TokenFlow pipeline minus keyframe editing; PSNR/LPIPS vs vanilla DDIM inversion and LDM autoencoder.
measured_outcome: PSNR/LPIPS: LDM recon 31.13/0.03, DDIM inversion 25.32/0.14, Ours 25.74/0.13.
direct_conclusion: Propagated tokens reconstruct frames slightly better than DDIM inversion; no direct test of correspondence correctness under occlusion.
author_hypothesis: Improvement due to keyframe randomisation.
confounders: Reconstruction is a proxy, not correspondence ground truth.
anchor: our evaluation focuses on accurate correspondences within the feature space during generation, rather than RGB frame correspondences evaluation

claim: With a large training corpus, unseen paintings are stylized with objective values close to seen paintings.
experiment: Model trained on PBN; style/content loss distributions over 2 photographs for 1024 observed vs 1024 unobserved paintings (Fig 3A).
measured_outcome: Observed: style 2.08e4 +/- 2.50e4, content 8.92e4 +/- 3.13e4. Unobserved: style 1.95e4 +/- 3.73e4, content 8.94e4 +/- 3.55e4. DTD-trained model on unobserved PBN: style 2.67e4 +/- 6.49e4, content 8.76e4 +/- 3.55e4.
direct_conclusion: Encoder-predicted state transfers to held-out paintings from the same distribution with similar mean loss; cross-domain (texture-trained) model shows higher mean and much larger variance of style loss.
author_hypothesis: The network learned a general method for artistic stylization.
confounders: Only 2 content photographs; loss is the training objective (Gram) itself; large standard deviations; held-out paintings come from the same PBN distribution.
anchor: The distribution of losses for observed styles (style: mean = 2.08e4 ± 2.50e4; content: mean = 8.92e4 ± 3.13e4)

claim: Generalization to unseen styles depends on training-corpus size: style loss on unseen paintings stays elevated until roughly 16,000 training paintings, while seen-style quality does not improve with corpus size.
experiment: Train networks on increasing numbers of paintings (no augmentation); loss distributions on unobserved paintings vs training paintings; qualitative stylizations of 3 unseen pairs vs a model trained explicitly on those styles (Fig 5).
measured_outcome: Style-loss distribution for unseen styles does not asymptote until ~16,000 paintings, after which it roughly matches trained-style losses; no significant change for training styles (plot values not in text).
direct_conclusion: Zero-shot reusability of the encoder is an acquired property of corpus scale, not of the CIN representation per se (consistent with Dumoulin's 32-style model not generalizing).
author_hypothesis: Generalization is largely due to training on far more paintings than before.
confounders: Numbers only in plot; 'roughly 16,000' is a visual reading by authors; no augmentation in this ablation unlike main model.
anchor: this distribution does not asymptote until roughly 16,000 paintings

claim: Unseen-style quality degrades with distance from the training set: style loss correlates with minimum Gram-space distance to training paintings.
experiment: Scatter of style loss on unobserved paintings vs min L2 Gram distance to all training Gram matrices (Fig 4; log-log Fig 5 supp) with easy/difficult examples (supp Fig 6).
measured_outcome: Positive correlation r^2 = 0.9; difficult (far) examples look slightly worse perceptually (qualitative).
direct_conclusion: Encoder-based reuse is reliable near the training distribution and weaker for out-of-distribution styles.
author_hypothesis: Difficult cases may lie in low-density regions of the embedding space (untested).
confounders: Gram distance and Gram style loss share the same feature space, which may inflate correlation.
anchor: The plot shows clear positive correlation (r2 = 0.9)

claim: Feed-forward arbitrary stylization trades objective value for speed: direct optimization reaches lower style loss on unseen paintings; the learned predictor beats AdaIN on the Gram objective.
experiment: Unobserved paintings: proposed vs Gatys optimization vs AdaIN, style/content losses; paired t-test vs AdaIN (Fig 3B,C).
measured_outcome: Style 1.95e4 (ours) vs 1.12e4 (Gatys); content 8.94e4 vs 9.09e4. Vs AdaIN: style 1.95e4 vs 2.56e4, content 8.94e4 vs 12.3e4; t-test style p=1.9e-9 (t=-6.04), content p=0.0 (t=-91.9).
direct_conclusion: Optimization achieves notably lower style loss than the amortized predictor; the AdaIN comparison is on the Gram objective the proposed model was trained on.
author_hypothesis: Learned mapping's flexibility yields better objective values than AdaIN's fixed heuristic mapping.
confounders: AdaIN was trained with a mean/std style loss, not this Gram loss (metric favours proposed model); different loss weights per method; no runtime measured; Gatys run with one parameter set for all images (supp A.3).
anchor: the proposed method obtains content and style losses that are comparable (style: 1.95e4 vs 1.12e4; content: 8.94e4 vs 9.09e4)

claim: Embedding space supports composition and strength control: feeding the content image as style yields an identity embedding, and interpolating toward an unseen painting dials stylization strength.
experiment: Interpolation between identity embedding and an unobserved painting's embedding (Fig 8); PCA-grid exploration of an artist cluster (Fig 7).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Linear operations on predicted embeddings produce plausible outputs in shown examples; no interference or quality measurement.
author_hypothesis: The model might capture a local manifold of an artist's style.
confounders: Cherry-picked examples; no metric.
anchor: supplying the network with a content image (i.e. photograph) produces an embedding that acts as the identity tranformation

claim: Full attention sharing among all images in a set causes cross-image content leakage (e.g. colour moving between siblings) and loss of diversity, yet it scores HIGHER on the DINO set-consistency metric.
experiment: 100 ChatGPT style prompts x 4 objects. Variants: StyleAligned (one reference, AdaIN Q/K), W.O. AdaIN, Full Attn. Share (all pairs share K/V). Metrics: CLIP text alignment; set consistency = mean pairwise DINO ViT-B/8 cosine. Plus qualitative Fig. 5 ('minimal flat design', 2 seeds).
measured_outcome: Table 2 (appendix) (CLIP / DINO): StyleAligned 0.287 +-0.03 / 0.51 +-0.14; W.O. AdaIN 0.289 +-0.03 / 0.428 +-0.14; Full Attn. 0.28 +-0.03 / 0.55 +-0.15. Fig. 5: unicorns get green paint from the dino in the same set.
direct_conclusion: Changing the routing (all-pairs vs one-reference sharing) changes leakage between generated siblings. The consistency metric rises with leakage, so a higher set consistency does not mean better style alignment. Removing Q/K AdaIN mostly lowers consistency (style dilution) with little text gain.
author_hypothesis: One-reference sharing without AdaIN aligns style poorly because too little attention flows from the reference to the target.
confounders: Here 'leakage' is between co-generated images, not from an external reference, and the leaked attribute (colour) could itself count as style. Standard deviations (~0.14) are large relative to the gaps. DINO similarity is a proxy that also rewards shared content.
locator: Sec. 3.2; Sec. 4.1; Fig. 5; Fig. 6; Appendix C, Table 2
anchor: full attention sharing results in content leakage among the images

claim: Single-image personalization baselines (StyleDrop-SDXL, DreamBooth-LoRA) reproduce reference objects. The authors explicitly link this leakage to their higher set-consistency and lower text scores. Encoder baselines show lower consistency.
experiment: Baselines trained or encoded on the first image of each set (StyleDrop and DB-LoRA trained 400 steps). The other 3 images are generated and the same CLIP/DINO metrics computed. Qualitative Fig. 7, encoder baselines in Fig. 23.
measured_outcome: Table 2 (CLIP / DINO): StyleDrop (SDXL) 0.272 / 0.529; StyleDrop (unofficial MUSE) 0.271 / 0.301; DreamBooth-LoRA (SDXL) 0.276 / 0.537; IP-Adapter (SDXL) 0.281 / 0.44; ELITE (SD 1.4) 0.253 / 0.481; BLIP-Diffusion (SD 1.4) 0.245 / 0.475; StyleAligned 0.287 / 0.51. Fig. 7: repeated woman-and-dogs and owl.
direct_conclusion: On this metric pair, leakage from the reference raises set consistency and lowers text alignment. So consistency scores cannot serve as style evidence unless leakage is controlled.
author_hypothesis: Encoder-based personalization methods have trouble separating content from style in the input image.
confounders: The backbones differ (SD 1.4 vs SDXL vs MUSE). Training steps were fixed at 400 rather than tuned per method. Leakage is identified only qualitatively. The CLIP text score covers only the object word.
locator: Sec. 4.2; Fig. 6; Fig. 7; Appendix C, Table 2, Fig. 23
anchor: because of the content leakage, these methods obtained lower text similarity scores and higher set consistency scores

claim: With very famous references, shared attention itself can copy the reference almost exactly and ignore the prompt. A routing tweak (rescaling the reference attention scores) is proposed to fix it, shown qualitatively only.
experiment: Real-image references via DDIM inversion (e.g. Starry Night, Tower of Babel). Rescaling of reference Q-K scores by lambda<1 varied (Fig. 15, values 1 and 0.75 visible).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 15). Without rescaling the output is almost identical to the reference; with rescaling the transfer is plausible.
direct_conclusion: Leakage of reference content under attention-based binding depends on the reference's activation and attention mass and can be reduced by reweighting attention. Whether the reduction trades off style strength is not shown.
author_hypothesis: Famous images produce high-confidence, high-magnitude activations, so the reference keys take most of the attention.
confounders: Untested explanation. No metric. Lambda is tuned per image. The rescaling may also dilute style.
anchor: the default approach may sometimes completely ignore the target prompt, generating an image almost identical to the reference

claim: StyleAligned counts composition and pose as style attributes, and its shared attention matches semantically corresponding regions. So reference structure transfer is partly intended, and the paper gives no operational line between leakage and style.
experiment: Attention-probability maps from target points to the reference (Fig. 10). PCA of shared attention maps (Fig. 11). Varying the share of layers with attention sharing (10/50/100%, Fig. 8).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only. Attention lands on semantically similar reference regions. Fewer shared layers give more varied images with weaker alignment.
direct_conclusion: Binding is correspondence-based, not a global statistic. The strength knob (fraction of shared layers) trades alignment for diversity rather than separating style from content.
author_hypothesis: Shared attention matches styles in a semantically meaningful way instead of performing global style transfer.
confounders: Hand-picked visualizations. The Fig. 8 knob is not quantified.
anchor: more consistent across style attributes like color palette, drawing style, composition, and pose

claim: Encoder-based arbitrary transfer runs at near per-style-network speed; style encoding is a separable, cacheable cost.
experiment: Runtime of AdaIN vs Gatys (500 it), Chen&Schmidt, Ulyanov, Dumoulin at 256 and 512; times excluding (including) style encoding; Pascal Titan X, averaged over 100 images (Table 1).
direct_conclusion: AdaIN's per-content cost is ~1.6-1.7x that of fixed-style networks and ~3 orders below optimization; style encoding adds ~50% when not cached.
author_hypothesis: Slower speed is due to the larger VGG-based network, not methodology.
confounders: Real-time FPS figures exclude style encoding; competing methods run with their default code/configurations; per-method training cost not included.
anchor: Excluding the time for style encoding, our algorithm runs at 56 and 15 FPS for 256 × 256

claim: On unseen styles, AdaIN's losses are slightly higher than per-style networks trained on each test style, but comparable; both match ~50-100 Gatys iterations.
experiment: 10 test styles x 50 content images (WikiArt test, MS-COCO); content and IN-statistics style loss vs Gatys iterations and Ulyanov per-style networks; Gatys/Ulyanov losses modified to IN statistics (Fig 3).
measured_outcome: Plot only: AdaIN slightly higher content and style loss than Ulyanov; both reach style loss similar to Gatys between 50 and 100 iterations.
direct_conclusion: Zero-shot encoder state approximates a per-style network's objective on unseen styles at a modest loss penalty, under this paper's mean/std metric.
author_hypothesis: Three-way trade-off between speed, flexibility and quality.
confounders: Metric is AdaIN's own training loss (mean/std); qualitative Fig 4 for baselines uses Gram loss; 10 styles; Ghiasi reports AdaIN worse on a Gram metric.
anchor: both our method and [52] obtain a style loss similar to that of [16] between 50 and 100 iterations

claim: Per-style quality cost of arbitrariness is visible in some cases: AdaIN is slightly behind per-style and optimization results on some styles.
experiment: Side-by-side results vs Chen&Schmidt, Ulyanov (fit per test style), Gatys on unseen styles, 512x512 (Fig 4).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (e.g., row 5 slightly behind)
direct_conclusion: Arbitrary-style generalization does not always match fitted per-style quality.
author_hypothesis: Three-way trade-off between speed, flexibility, and quality.
confounders: Visual judgement; selected rows.
anchor: In some other cases (e.g., row 5) our method is slightly behind the quality of [52] and [16]

claim: Binding matters for reference-content leakage: concatenating content and style features lets style-image object contours appear in outputs; AdaIN binding does not show this in the example.
experiment: Enc-AdaIN-Dec vs Enc-Concat-Dec (and BN/IN decoders), same training settings; example images (Fig 5) and training loss curves (Fig 6).
measured_outcome: Concat: object contours of style image clearly visible; reaches low style loss but fails to decrease content loss (curves). BN/IN decoders: consistently higher losses.
direct_conclusion: Replacing statistics-based binding with concatenation produced visible reference-content leakage in the shown example, accompanied by a high content loss.
author_hypothesis: Concat network fails to disentangle style information from the content of the style image.
confounders: Single qualitative example; no leakage metric; leakage co-occurs with target-content distortion (high content loss), so the two are not separated.
anchor: the object contours of the style image can be clearly observed, suggesting that the network fails to disentangle

claim: Runtime controls (content-style trade-off, style interpolation, spatial and colour control) work without retraining by manipulating AdaIN features.
experiment: Feature interpolation alpha (Eq.14, Fig 7); convex combination of AdaIN outputs for K styles (Eq.15, Fig 8); region-wise AdaIN with masks (Fig 10); colour-preserved style image (Fig 9).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Composition of multiple arbitrary styles is feasible at test time; no interference measurement; decoder trained only on homogeneous styles still produced plausible mixed-region outputs in shown example.
author_hypothesis: Decoder generalizes naturally to inputs with region-wise different styles.
confounders: Selected examples only.
anchor: Note that all these controls are only applied at runtime using the same network

claim: For video, cached style statistics are reused across frames, but no temporal-consistency evaluation is performed.
experiment: None.
measured_outcome: No temporal metric.
direct_conclusion: Shared style condition across frames is an efficiency property, not a consistency guarantee.
anchor: the style image needs to be encoded only once and AdaIN can use the stored style statistics

claim: Per-style feed-forward networks amortize the Gatys optimization: inference is ~2x faster than one baseline iteration and ~1000x faster than 500 iterations, under matched GPU.
experiment: Runtime of the per-style network vs reimplemented projected L-BFGS Gatys baseline at 100/300/500 iterations, image sizes 256, 512, 1024; both on a GTX Titan X (Table 1).
direct_conclusion: Once a style network is trained, per-content inference cost is ~3 orders of magnitude below 500-iteration optimization at the same resolution and hardware.
confounders: Excludes ~4 h per-style training cost; baseline is the authors' reimplementation with clipping (projected L-BFGS); 500 iterations is an assumed convergence point.
anchor: Compared to 500 iterations of the baseline method, our method is three orders of magnitude faster

claim: The amortized network does not reach the optimizer's objective value: its loss is comparable to only 50-100 iterations of explicit optimization, at all tested resolutions.
experiment: 50 MS-COCO val images, one style (The Muse, Picasso); objective value of Eq.5 for network output vs baseline loss per iteration; repeated at 512 and 1024 (Fig 5).
measured_outcome: Network loss comparable to between 50 and 100 L-BFGS iterations (exact values only in plot; not readable from text).
direct_conclusion: Speed is bought with a higher objective value than converged optimization (500 iterations); training at 256 generalizes to larger inputs at a similar relative level.
author_hypothesis: Qualitative results are 'similar' to the baseline.
confounders: Single style; objective value is a proxy for perceptual quality; hyperparameters matched between methods.
