anchor: our method achieves a loss comparable to between 50 and 100 iterations of explicit optimization

claim: Style state is non-portable across styles: one network is trained per style target, with TV strength cross-validated per style.
experiment: Training protocol description.
measured_outcome: Training ~4 hours per style on one GTX Titan X; 40,000 iterations batch 4 on 80k COCO images; TV strength 1e-6 to 1e-4 chosen per style.
direct_conclusion: Adding a new style requires a full training run; nothing from previous styles is reused except architecture.
confounders: Training time is approximate and hardware-specific.
anchor: with the style of ys ; we train one network per style target

claim: Stylization distorts content unevenly: people and animal faces remain recognizable while backgrounds are warped, attributed to VGG-16 class selectivity.
experiment: 512x512 examples (Fig 7), beach and cat images.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Target-content distortion depends on image semantics as encoded by the loss network, not uniformly on the style weight.
author_hypothesis: VGG-16 features are selective for people and animals because these appear in its classification dataset.
confounders: Two examples; no controlled loss-network variation.
anchor: the people are clearly recognizable in the transformed image but the background is warped beyond recognition

claim: Real-time video applicability is asserted from frame rate only; temporal consistency is not tested.
experiment: None for video; claim derived from 20 FPS at 512x512.
measured_outcome: 20 FPS at 512x512 (Titan X); no temporal metric.
direct_conclusion: Speed permits per-frame processing, but nothing constrains frame-to-frame consistency.
author_hypothesis: Feasible to run style transfer in real-time or on video.
anchor: making it feasible to run style transfer in real-time or on video

claim: The authors show that CLIP/DINO image-similarity 'style' metrics favour outputs with higher semantic similarity to the reference, i.e. they reward reference-content leakage, so they decline to use them as style scores.
experiment: Two prompts ('A snowy mountain peak.', 'A cute little fish in aquarium.') x 8 methods; per-image CLIP and DINO similarity to the style reference displayed under each output.
measured_outcome: Per-image CLIP/DINO scores are printed in Fig. 14 but the method-to-score mapping is TABLE_TEXT_GARBLED in the text extraction; no aggregate reported.
direct_conclusion: On two displayed examples, outputs the authors judge as leaking reference content receive higher CLIP/DINO similarity; this is a two-example illustration, not a systematic metric study.
author_hypothesis: Higher semantic similarity does not indicate better style preservation and can weaken style.
confounders: Two examples chosen by authors; 'leakage' judged visually; no alternative leakage metric proposed; style quality evaluated only by user study.
anchor: They tend to favor higher semantic similarity to the style image rather than better style transfer

claim: Changing the fusion operator (weighted sum -> cross-modal AdaIN) and adding teacher layout sharing increases CLIP text alignment on 'A <color> <object>' prompts, i.e. less style overfitting of colour/content to the reference.
experiment: Benchmark: 52 prompts (StyleAdapter set; 30 additional 'A <color> <object>' prompts by ChatGPT) x 20 StyleShot style images, 1,000 images per method; CLIP image-text cosine similarity; CSGO baseline with/without cross-modal AdaIN and Teacher Model; fixed seed 42, guidance 5, 50 steps.
measured_outcome: Table 2 text alignment: baseline 0.216; Teacher only 0.223 (+3.2%); Cross-modal AdaIN only 0.228 (+5.5%); both 0.235 (+8.7%). (Row-component assignment from prose: teacher alone 'initial enhancement', AdaIN 'more significant'.)
direct_conclusion: Both binding changes raise CLIP text alignment with CSGO as base; no style-similarity metric is reported for the same ablation, so whether the gain is partly style dilution is not measured.
author_hypothesis: Additive fusion forces text and image to play similar roles and creates conflicts; AdaIN lets text define content while style supplies statistics.
confounders: CLIP text score is a prompt-adherence proxy, not a leakage or style metric; style strength under AdaIN only checked qualitatively (Fig. 17) and via user study on the full model; colour-word prompts specifically target colour overfitting.
anchor: Incorporating the Teacher Model alone provides an initial enhancement, while cross-modal AdaIN yields a more significant improvement

claim: Layout constraint from an unstylised teacher trades off against style: too few teacher steps leave layout instability/duplicates; teacher over all 50 steps visibly dilutes style. Optimal cutoff varies by style.
experiment: Teacher participation for 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 50 of 50 steps, without cross-modal AdaIN; also on InstantStyle and StyleCrafter; qualitative grids.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 9, Fig. 19, Fig. 22, Fig. 23)
direct_conclusion: Self-attention-map sharing reduces layout artifacts but causes style dilution with long participation in displayed examples; recommended cutoff 10-20 steps.
author_hypothesis: Checkerboard/layout instability correlates with scattered cross-attention for the object word (Fig. 5, Fig. 8).
confounders: No metric per cutoff; examples selected; 'optimal timestep can vary across different styles' means a per-style tuning knob.
anchor: an extended involvement can dilute the style elements, making it essential to find a balanced point to discontinue its

claim: Content leakage in StyleCrafter and IP-Adapter is linked by the authors to layout disruption, and imposing the teacher's self-attention layout on StyleCrafter visibly reduces leakage, a binding change on spatial structure rather than on the style representation.
experiment: Teacher Model inserted into StyleCrafter for varying step counts; qualitative comparison with 'A red apple' prompts; cross-method comparison grids (Fig. 24-26).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 23, Fig. 26)
direct_conclusion: In displayed examples, constraining layout via self-attention maps of an unconditioned pass reduces visible reference elements; not quantified and not separated from style weakening.
author_hypothesis: Content leakage is a form of overfitting to the style reference and is closely related to layout disruptions.
confounders: Teacher at long participation also dilutes style (record above), so leakage reduction and dilution are not disentangled; no leakage metric.
locator: Appendix D; Appendix F.2; Fig. 23; Fig. 26
anchor: Notably, content leakage appears to be closely related to layout disruptions

claim: Style-factor entanglement: a single reference carries multiple style elements (e.g., cartoon + night/snow/golden leaves); negative-style-image CFG suppresses unwanted elements where a negative text prompt fails, shown only on examples.
experiment: Baseline vs + negative text prompt vs + negative style image (ControlNet-generated) on several references; CFG weight 5-8 variations (Fig. 15).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 7, Fig. 15)
direct_conclusion: In displayed examples, image-space negative guidance removes specific unwanted elements better than text negatives.
author_hypothesis: Current methods cannot disentangle multiple style elements and selectively emphasise one.
confounders: Negative images hand-crafted per reference ('requires expertise and manual effort'); no metric; not included in the quantitative Table 1 runs (only AdaIN + Teacher used there).
anchor: generating negative-style image requires expertise and manual effort

claim: Training-free fixes add per-sample compute: full method 17 s vs CSGO 9 s per image; SCFG adds manual per-reference negative-image creation.
experiment: Table 1 inference time on a single GPU (stated GTX-4090) alongside text alignment and user study (49 users, 12 reference-prompt pairs).
measured_outcome: Table 1: text alignment / time (s) / user text % / user style %: IP-Adapter 0.221 / 6 / 7.48 / 6.63; InstantStyle 0.229 / 6 / 6.46 / 8.67; CSGO 0.216 / 9 / 7.99 / 6.97; StyleAlign 0.180 / 48 / 5.78 / 7.82; StyleCrafter 0.189 / 4 / 3.06 / 8.67; StyleShot 0.202 / 3 / 2.55 / 5.10; DEADiff 0.229 / 2 / 1.87 / 5.27; Ours 0.235 / 17 / 62.92 / 50.85.
direct_conclusion: The teacher pass roughly doubles CSGO's inference time; text alignment gain over InstantStyle/DEADiff is 0.006.
confounders: User study forced single choice among 8 methods on 12 pairs; no objective style metric; IP-Adapter run 'with weight tuning'.
anchor: For each method’s generated images, 49 users participated in an anonymous vote

claim: Style-agnostic decoders remove style-specific training entirely; new styles need only feature statistics, at a moderate runtime cost relative to single-pass feed-forward methods.
experiment: Run-time at 256x256 on a 12GB TITAN X for Chen et al., Huang (AdaIN), TNet, Gatys, Ours (Table 2, 3rd row).
measured_outcome: Time/sec: Chen 2.1, Huang 0.20, TNet 0.18, Gatys 21.2, Ours 0.83.
direct_conclusion: WCT is ~4x slower than AdaIN/TNet in this setup and ~25x faster than optimization, with no per-style training.
author_hypothesis: Eigendecomposition cost does not grow with image size since covariance dimension depends only on channel count; GPU implementation would speed it up.
confounders: Eigendecomposition run on CPU; AdaIN time (0.20s) is ~10x higher than AdaIN's own report (0.018s) under a similar GPU, indicating implementation differences; size-independence of decomposition cost is asserted, not measured.
anchor: a little bit slower than [27, 15] because we have a eigenvalue decomposition step in WCT
review_note: Main reader: runtime of AdaIN measured by WCT (0.20 s) vs AdaIN self-report (0.018 s / 0.027 s with encoding) is the F1.6 non-identifiability example.

claim: WCT obtains the lowest covariance-based style loss and most user votes among five methods; but the metric is the statistic WCT directly matches.
experiment: log(Ls) over 5 VGG levels for 10 content x 40 style images; user study 5 content x 30 styles, 80 subjects, 1,200 votes choosing one favourite (Table 2).
measured_outcome: log(Ls): Chen 7.4, Huang 7.0, TNet 6.8, Gatys 6.7, Ours 6.3. Preference %: 15.7, 24.9, 12.7, 16.4, 30.3.
direct_conclusion: Under covariance matching and a forced-choice preference, learning-free WCT is not worse than per-style or optimization baselines; AdaIN received the second-most votes.
author_hypothesis: AdaIN is a sub-optimal approximation of WCT.
confounders: Ls is covariance difference, which WCT matches by construction; each baseline's style weight adjusted 'to obtain the best stylized effect' (subjective tuning); Gatys local minima shown; TNet is the 2016 Texture Networks, not improved version.
anchor: Quantitative results show that we generate stylized results with lower Ls , i.e., closer to the statistics of the style

claim: Style-statistic richness affects style dilution: mean/variance (AdaIN) and channel-wise histogram matching fail to reproduce salient patterns, while full covariance captures them.
experiment: HM vs WCT within the same multi-level framework (Fig 3); comparison with AdaIN and others on paintings and texton styles (Fig 6).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Feature statistics lacking cross-channel correlation transfer global colour but break local structure in shown examples (style dilution/entanglement of colour vs pattern).
author_hypothesis: HM ignores channel correlations that the covariance encodes.
confounders: Selected examples; style weights of baselines tuned by authors; AdaIN in Fig 6 trained on WikiArt while test styles may differ.
anchor: the HM method helps transfer the global color of the style image well but fails to capture salient visual patterns

claim: Whitening removes style-related detail while preserving global content structure of the image being whitened.
experiment: Decode whitened relu4_1 features with reconstruction decoder for two images (Fig 2).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: The whitened content representation keeps global layout; stroke patterns of a painting are removed in the example. Does not measure reference leakage in stylized outputs.
author_hypothesis: Whitening peels off style from an input image.
confounders: Two examples; pixel intensities rescaled for visualization.
anchor: the whitened features still maintain global structures of the image contents, but greatly help remove other information related to styles

claim: Feature-space blending supports test-time strength, scale, spatial control and texture interpolation; feature blending yields new textures where Gram-loss blending overlays them.
experiment: alpha blending (Eq.4, Fig 7), style image rescaling (Fig 7), masks (Fig 8), texture interpolation beta vs Gatys weighted Gram loss (Fig 10).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Composition at the feature level and at the loss level behave differently in the shown example; no interference metric.
author_hypothesis: Loss-level blending may not always lead to a good balance point.
confounders: Single texture pair; subjective.
anchor: the result by [9] is simply overlaid by two textures while our method generates new textural effects

claim: Affinity preservation is a within-frame property proven for any linear transform; it does not constrain correspondence between frames, so temporal stability is an inferred, not enforced, consequence.
experiment: Derivation: normalized affinity aff(F) = F^T cov(F)^-1 F; shown aff(F_d) = aff(F_c) under F_d = T F_c.
measured_outcome: Mathematical identity (eq. 4-5); no temporal quantity appears. Authors add that decoder depth, the loss-dependent trace term and top-layer resolution still cause distortion, motivating a shallower relu3_1 model.
direct_conclusion: The guarantee concerns pairwise relations among pixels of one frame at the bottleneck; frame-to-frame stability additionally requires that T (which depends on per-frame content covariance) and the nonlinear decoder respond smoothly to input change, which is not proven.
author_hypothesis: Because content videos are naturally consistent and affinity is preserved, stylized videos are stable without optical flow warping.
confounders: T contains a content-covariance branch recomputed per frame; decoder is nonlinear; affinity identity is at feature resolution, not pixel level.
anchor: our stylized videos are also visually stable without the aid of any auxiliary techniques, such as optical flow

claim: Video stability evidence is limited to a two-frame difference heat map and a stability-preference user study; no warping error or flow-based metric is reported.
experiment: Frame-wise video stylization (relu3_1 model) vs Gatys, Johnson, WCT (Fig. 7: frames 1 and 5, heat map of difference); user study with 5 clips per group vs Gatys, Ulyanov, AdaIN, WCT, subjects pick most stable clip.
measured_outcome: Heat map: qualitative figure only (authors state theirs is closest to the input-frame difference). User study: 106 votes from 27 subjects; Fig. 8(b) pie percentages TABLE_TEXT_GARBLED (an 81.8% slice appears, likely for the proposed method, but assignment cannot be verified from text).
direct_conclusion: Human raters preferred the method's clips for stability in this small study; no correspondence-based or occlusion-aware measurement, no fidelity measurement on the same clips.
author_hypothesis: Similarity of output difference map to input difference map indicates preserved content affinity.
confounders: Video results use the shallower relu3_1 model, which the authors say is less expressive for abstract styles (weaker stylization operating point), while baselines run at their default strength; 5 clips; stability judged without style-strength question.
anchor: we ask each subject to select the most stable video clip. We collect 106 votes from 27 subjects

claim: The configuration used for stable video trades stylization strength: relu3_1 bottleneck chosen to avoid instabilities but is noted as less expressive for abstract styles.
experiment: Ablation of bottleneck depth (relu3_1 vs relu4_1) and style-loss layers (Fig. 5); task-specific choice described in text.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Stability claims for video rest on a weaker-stylizing, structure-preserving operating point; stability and stylization strength are not reported jointly.
author_hypothesis: Lower-layer content features and shallower decoders produce fewer distortions.
confounders: No quantitative style metric.
locator: Section 3.4 (last sentence); Section 5.2 'Combining multi-level style losses'; Fig. 5
anchor: for photo-realistic and video style transfer, we transfer content image features from relu3 1 to avoid distortions and instabilities

claim: A single trained model serves arbitrary styles; per style only one style-branch pass is needed and reused across all video frames.
experiment: Run time on Titan XP at 256/512/1024 px vs Ulyanov, Gatys, AdaIN, WCT (Table 1).
direct_conclusion: Per-style cost is a feed-forward pass; nothing per style is optimized. Style-branch reuse across frames is by construction (not separately timed).
confounders: Run times from original source code of each method; Ulyanov is not arbitrary-style.
anchor: output in the style branch can be computed only once during initialization (see Figure 2), and then directly applied

claim: The paper itself states that warping error is won by static output: VideoComposer, which often produces static videos, has the lowest warping error; no motion-magnitude control is reported.
experiment: Single-reference style-guided T2V on 240 single-reference pairs (12 prompts x 20 styles): VideoComposer, VideoCrafter* (GPT-4V style prompt), Ours. Metrics: CLIP-Text, CLIP-Style, CLIP-Temp (cosine similarity of CLIP embeddings of consecutive frames), warping error with RAFT-small flow.
direct_conclusion: Warping error ranks a near-static, reference-copying generator best; CLIP-Temp also ranks it close to the proposed method. Neither temporal metric controls for amount of motion.
author_hypothesis: VideoComposer's low warping error does not mean best temporal quality; users judge temporal quality including presence of motion.
confounders: No motion/dynamics metric; generated content differs across methods (no shared source video), so warping error compares different scenes; CLIP-Style inflated by reference copying.
anchor: VideoComposer often generates static videos, thus having the lowest warping errors, but this does not mean

claim: Temporal consistency is enforced only by the base model's temporal self-attention prior (fine-tuned with the adapter); the shared per-frame style condition is not a correspondence constraint, and no correspondence is used in training.
experiment: Method description: style embedding F_s injected identically into all frames via SCA; stage 2 fine-tunes temporal blocks on WebVid + stylized images with denoising loss only.
measured_outcome: No flow, tracking or cross-frame correspondence term; evaluation uses RAFT-small flow estimated on generated frames (no occlusion mask stated) and CLIP frame similarity.
direct_conclusion: The metric's correspondence (RAFT-small on outputs) has no counterpart in the mechanism; consistency is an emergent property of the learned temporal prior. A shared style condition constrains global appearance statistics across frames, not point-wise appearance along trajectories.
author_hypothesis: Without temporal adaptation, cross-frame temporal self-attention is incompatible with stylized features, causing jitter.
locator: Section 3.1 eq. (1); Section 3.2; Supplement B.1 eq. (5),(6)
anchor: we first obtain the optical flow between each two frames using RAFT-small

claim: Fine-tuning temporal blocks after adapter training improves both temporal metrics and style score; here consistency gains do not come from weaker style.
experiment: Ablation on two-stage scheme: w/o temporal adaption (image-trained adapter applied directly), joint training of adapter and temporal blocks, two-stage (ours); same T2V test set.
measured_outcome: Table 5 (CLIP-Text / CLIP-Style / CLIP-Temp / W.E. x10^-3): w/o Temporal Adaption 0.2691/0.3923/0.9612/47.88; Joint Training 0.3138/0.2226/0.9741/24.74; Two-Stage 0.2726/0.4531/0.9892/18.73.
direct_conclusion: Adapting temporal blocks to the style adapter lowers warping error (47.88 to 18.73) and raises CLIP-Temp while CLIP-Style rises; joint training weakens style (0.2226) without achieving the best consistency.
author_hypothesis: Joint fine-tuning interferes with learning the style embedding extraction.
confounders: Motion amount not measured, so lower warping error could partly reflect less motion; adjacent frames only; single base model.
anchor: baseline (i) exhibits inferior temporal consistency when applied directly to video, and undermines the content alignment
review_note: Main reader: counterexample to the consistency-fidelity trade-off sub-claim (F3.3).

claim: Human judgments of temporal quality do not follow the proposed method's metric lead: Gen-2* is preferred over StyleCrafter on temporal quality in single-reference comparisons.
experiment: User study, 15 users, 15 single-reference pairs (VideoCrafter*, Gen-2*, Ours) and 10 multi-reference pairs (AnimateDiff vs Ours M-R); text alignment, style conformity, temporal quality (requires motion and no flicker); 1125 votes.
direct_conclusion: Users preferred Gen-2* for temporal quality (51.1% vs 44.4%); Gen-2* is absent from the quantitative Table 2, so metric-vs-human agreement cannot be checked for it.
author_hypothesis: Gen-2 is more prone to sudden changes in color and luminance (qualitative claim).
confounders: Small user study; temporal question mixes motion presence and coherence; VideoComposer excluded from user study.
anchor: Temporal Quality (single choice, consists of two aspects

claim: Routing style through text cross-attention (attach-to-text) leaks reference content and destroys text alignment; dual cross-attention reduces this, but the CLIP-Style metric rewards the leaking variant.
experiment: Style-guided T2I ablation on 400 pairs: Ours vs w/o data augmentation vs w/o dual cross-attention (attach-to-text) vs w/o adaptive fusion; CLIP-Text, CLIP-Style; Fig. 7 qualitative.
measured_outcome: Table 4 (CLIP-Text / CLIP-Style): Ours 0.3028/0.4836; w/o Data Augmentation 0.3173/0.4005; w/o Dual Cross Attention 0.0983/0.7332; w/o Adaptive Fusion 0.2807/0.4925.
direct_conclusion: Changing the binding route changes reference-content leakage as measured by collapsed text alignment and inflated style similarity; reduced leakage coincides with a lower CLIP-Style, so the style metric cannot distinguish leakage from fidelity. Removing crop augmentation lowers style score (dilution) rather than increasing leakage.
author_hypothesis: Attach-to-text fuses content from the reference image with the prompt rather than combining text content with image style; authors acknowledge copying the reference yields close-to-1 style score.
confounders: No direct leakage metric (e.g. object detection of reference content); same guidance scales for all variants.
anchor: attach-to-text tends to directly fuse the content from the reference image and the text prompts

claim: A single tuning-free adapter outperforms per-style DreamBooth+AnimateDiff on style score with multi-reference inputs, but the adapter is bound to the base model's spatial weights.
experiment: 60 multi-reference text-style pairs; AnimateDiff with a DreamBooth model trained per style (1500 steps) vs Ours with single or concatenated multiple references.
direct_conclusion: Per-style fine-tuned assets combined with pre-trained temporal blocks underperformed here; the generic adapter needs no per-style optimisation. Portability to another backbone (SDXL) required retraining stage 1.
author_hypothesis: Incompatibility between pre-trained temporal blocks and independently trained personalised SD both breaks temporal consistency and weakens style.
confounders: DreamBooth on SD 1.5 vs adapter on VideoCrafter/SD 2.1 (different backbones); AnimateDiff with LoRA not used because it failed in most cases.
locator: Section 4.3 'Multi-Reference based Guidance'; Table 2; Section 4.1; Supplement A.1
anchor: we conjecture that the performance degradation is caused by the incompatibility from the pre-trained temporal blocks
review_note: Main reader: a shared multi-reference adapter beats per-style DreamBooth fitting on style score, so greater style-specificity of the acquired state is not monotonically higher fidelity. Recoded from qualifies to counterexample after F1.1 was narrowed to include less-shared learned states.

claim: Per-style cost is a single 0.105 s transfer with no optimisation, while scene-specific embedding and decoder training are the acquired state that must be redone per scene.
experiment: Transfer and rendering time vs HyperNet and StyleRF (excluding IO), Tanks and Temples and Mip-NeRF 360 scenes.
measured_outcome: Transfer time (s): HyperNet 1.908, StyleRF 3.403, StyleGaussian 0.105. Rendering time (s): HyperNet 32.373, StyleRF 10.084, StyleGaussian 0.005. Per-scene training reported only as iterations (embedding 30,000; decoder 100,000), no wall-clock.
direct_conclusion: Style changes are cheap once a scene is prepared; the paper itself names per-scene training as time-consuming but does not quantify it.
author_hypothesis: Speed comes from transferring the whole 3D representation once and decoding in 3D.
confounders: Different underlying scene representations (NeRF++, TensoRF, 3DGS) dominate rendering-time differences; GPU is an RTX A5000; Gaussians capped at 3x10^5.
locator: Section 5.2; Table 1; Section 5.4 'Decoder initialization'; Appendix A
anchor: StyleGaussian, is the requirement for timeconsuming pre-scene training. To mitigate this issue

claim: The decoder is scene-bound but partially portable: initialising from another scene's decoder reaches similar results with less than one third of training.
experiment: Decoder trained on scene (a) used to initialise scene (b), fine-tuned (30,000 iterations) vs trained from scratch (100,000 iterations).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 9); iterations 30,000 vs 100,000.
direct_conclusion: Cross-scene reuse of the decoder as initialisation reduces, but does not remove, per-scene acquisition.
confounders: Single scene pair; no quantitative similarity measure.
anchor: This initialization process allows us to achieve similar stylization results with less than 1/3 of the training time.

claim: Multi-view consistency is enforced by construction (fixed per-Gaussian colours) and measured with flow-warped LPIPS/RMSE; long-range advantage over HyperNet is small.
experiment: Warp one rendered stylized view to another with RAFT optical flow and softmax splatting; masked LPIPS and RMSE for short- and long-range view pairs.
measured_outcome: Short-range LPIPS/RMSE: HyperNet 0.036/0.043, StyleRF 0.050/0.045, StyleGaussian 0.026/0.031. Long-range LPIPS/RMSE: HyperNet 0.076/0.078, StyleRF 0.123/0.098, StyleGaussian 0.072/0.073.
direct_conclusion: StyleGaussian has the lowest warp errors; long-range errors remain non-zero and close to HyperNet's.
author_hypothesis: 2D CNN decoding (StyleRF) and view-dependency (HyperNet) impair consistency; 3D decoding preserves strict consistency.
confounders: Flow-warping error and occlusion masks set a non-zero floor even for 'strict' consistency; number of view pairs/scenes not stated; view-dependency omitted in StyleGaussian's stylized colours.
anchor: we warp one view to another according to the optical flow [44] using softmax splatting

claim: Style expression depends on the decoder's receptive field: a per-point MLP decoder fails to transfer strokes/texture, PointNet gives uniform colour.
experiment: Decoder ablation: KNN 3D CNN vs MLP vs PointNet (Fig. 6); content-style weight lambda in {1,3,5,10} at training (Fig. 7).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: With the same AdaIN statistics, binding through a small-receptive-field decoder yields style dilution (colour without stroke/texture patterns).
author_hypothesis: A large receptive field is required to decode stylized RGB.
confounders: Qualitative; lambda fixed at training (lambda=10 chosen visually), so the trade-off is not an inference-time control.
anchor: its per-point receptive field size limits its ability to transfer more general style patterns like strokes and texture

claim: Consistency is obtained by freezing geometry, so geometric style (distortions) cannot be transferred and scene size is memory-limited.
experiment: Limitations section.
measured_outcome: Gaussians limited to 3 x 10^5 for 24G memory (stated); no geometry stylization.
direct_conclusion: The consistency guarantee covers colour on a fixed shared geometry only.
anchor: StyleGaussian only modifies the color of 3D Gaussians but leaves the geometry unchanged.

claim: Stylos reports the best short- and long-range warped LPIPS/RMSE on four scenes, but the flow estimator, frame gaps, view split and occlusion masking are not specified, and evaluation resolutions differ across methods.
experiment: Short/long-range LPIPS and RMSE 'following Chiang et al. 2022' on Train, Truck, M60, Garden vs StyleGaussian, G-Style, SGSST, Styl3R; 50 unseen styles.
measured_outcome: Short-range LPIPS/RMSE Train: StyleGaussian 0.033/0.038, Stylos 0.030/0.026. Long-range Truck: StyleGaussian 0.086/0.077, Styl3R 0.116/0.100, Stylos 0.074/0.069. Garden long-range: Styl3R 0.146/0.145, Stylos 0.139/0.134.
direct_conclusion: Under the authors' (under-specified) protocol, Stylos has lower warped error than the compared methods in every listed cell.
author_hypothesis: Global CrossBlock plus voxel-level 3D style loss enforce view-consistent stylization.
confounders: Per-scene 3DGS methods evaluated at full resolution, Styl3R at 256x256, Stylos at 448x448 (lower resolution can lower warped error). Correspondence source unstated. Garden is listed among 'Tanks & Temples' scenes.
anchor: following prior work (Chiang et al., 2022), we compute LPIPS and RMSE in both short-range and long-range settings

claim: The authors explicitly acknowledge that degenerate near-uniform-colour stylizations improve warped-consistency scores, and exclude such StylizedGS failures, showing the metric can reward weak stylization.
experiment: Reproduction of StylizedGS on the 50 test styles; failure cases excluded from consistency and ArtScore computation.
measured_outcome: Statement only: failures produce 'pure colors with barely visible' geometry and significantly improve consistency scores; StylizedGS numbers moved to Tables 5-6.
direct_conclusion: Warped-error consistency is not meaningful without a joint style-fidelity control; exclusion was a manual judgement.
confounders: Exclusion criterion for 'failure' not defined quantitatively.
anchor: It significantly improves its consistency scores in our experiments

claim: Changing the style loss from per-image to voxel-level barely changes measured consistency while ArtScore nearly doubles, so the 3D loss's consistency benefit is not clearly measured.
experiment: CO3D, 15 held-out scenes, frame stride 3; image-level vs scene-level vs voxel-level style loss; short/long-range LPIPS/RMSE and ArtScore.
direct_conclusion: Consistency differences are within ~0.001-0.006; the main effect of the scene/3D losses is stronger stylization. The image loss 'may fail to transfer style' yet has nearly equal consistency.
author_hypothesis: Voxel-level enforcement yields more coherent stylized textures across views.
confounders: Consistency of a weakly stylized (image-loss) output is not penalised; no variance reported.
anchor: We observe that the image-level supervision may fail to transfer style

claim: Geometry is predicted by a style-independent pathway frozen during stylization training, so style cannot alter geometry by construction; geometric reconstruction quality is the stated failure source.
experiment: Architecture (Sec. 3.2.3) and training (Stage 2 freezes geometry modules); limitations section.
measured_outcome: Style-free reconstruction PSNR on CO3D (Global CrossBlock): Skateboard 21.68, Pizza 20.57, Donut 22.09 dB (Table 1). Limitations: failures from inaccurate reconstruction, degradation as view count grows (VGGT instability).
direct_conclusion: Consistency is bounded by feed-forward geometry quality; stylized geometric fidelity is not separately measured.
author_hypothesis: Performance drop with many views stems from VGGT backbone instability.
confounders: Reconstruction PSNR uses the first frame as pseudo-style, not real styles.
anchor: information directly into Gaussian colors while leaving the geometry parameters pm unaffected

claim: All acquired state is in one network trained once; per-style and per-scene cost is a single forward pass, versus minutes of per-scene fitting for 3DGS baselines, but style fidelity metrics do not uniformly favour Stylos.
experiment: Stylization time on one GH200 GPU (per-scene methods include training time) and ArtScore/ArtFID on four scenes.
measured_outcome: Time: StyleGaussian 165 m, G-Style 14.7 m, SGSST 35.2 m, Styl3R 0.16 s, Stylos 0.05 s. ArtFID Train/Truck/M60/Garden: G-Style 23.24/22.15/22.36/25.76, Stylos 26.40/28.71/27.44/28.06.
direct_conclusion: Feed-forward reuse eliminates per-scene/per-style adaptation; G-Style (per-scene, per-style) has better ArtFID in all four scenes.
author_hypothesis: Stylos offers a favourable balance of quality, consistency and efficiency.
confounders: Training cost of Stylos excluded from time; resolutions differ across methods; Stylos trained on DL3DV scenes and style datasets.
locator: Section 4.2; Table 4 and footnotes; Appendix A.4
anchor: For methods with per-scene fitting required, the training phase accounts towards stylization time

claim: Consistency is measured by RAFT-flow warped error between novel-view frames, with flow and occlusion computed on photorealistic views from the pre-trained (unstylized) NeRF, averaged over 12 styles.
experiment: Test videos of novel views on 4 Tanks and Temples scenes; flow + occlusion mask from two ground-truth views rendered by the pre-trained NeRF via RAFT; masked squared error between warped stylized view and stylized view; short-range (i, i+1) and long-range (i, i+7). Compared against AdaIN, WCT, LST, ReReVST, MCCNet.
direct_conclusion: SNeRF has lower short-range warped error than per-frame image methods and is comparable to the video method ReReVST (better on 3 of 4 scenes, worse on M60).
author_hypothesis: Implicit scene representation provides a strong inductive bias for cross-view consistency.
confounders: SNeRF changes density/geometry, yet flow and occlusion come from the unstylized NeRF, so the metric's correspondence may not match the stylized geometry. No 3D baseline (StyleScene, Chiang et al.) is in the table. Style strength not jointly measured; tables are mislabelled 'Qualitative comparisons'.
anchor: we use RAFT [Teed and Deng 2021], a state-of-the-art method to predict optical flow

claim: At long range a 2D video method (ReReVST) beats the 3D-representation method on two of four scenes, so a shared NeRF did not uniformly dominate long-range warped consistency.
experiment: Same protocol as Table 1 with frame gap 7.
direct_conclusion: ReReVST is lower on Truck and M60, SNeRF lower on Playground and Train; authors concede ReReVST is competitive but argue it captures style worse (user study).
author_hypothesis: ReReVST does not capture the reference style well, so its consistency is cheaper.
confounders: Consistency and style fidelity measured separately (user study, 35 participants); a weaker-stylized output can score better on warped error. Gap of 7 frames only; flow from unstylized NeRF views.
anchor: that ReReVST produces competitive results with our method
review_note: SNeRF beats both 2D video baselines on short-range error in all four scenes (Table 1); ReReVST is lower on long-range error in two of four (Table 2). | Main reader: contradicts a naive claim that shared 3D scenes dominate long-range consistency; supports the F3 scope claim.

claim: Stylization deliberately alters geometry (density); freezing density limits results to colour scheme, but no geometric-fidelity metric is reported.
experiment: Ablation: freeze shared/opacity branches (appearance only) vs stylize geometry+appearance; qualitative.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 9)
direct_conclusion: Geometry is part of what SNeRF stylizes; consistency of a changed geometry is not separately verified.
author_hypothesis: Geometry is a component of style; stylizing it gives results closer to the target style.
confounders: Abstract styles cherry-picked; no measurement of geometric distortion or of whether the evaluation flow remains valid after geometry change.
anchor: our method stylizes both the appearance and geometry (represented as density) of the scene functions

claim: Fitting a NeRF once to inconsistent per-view stylizations already yields cross-view consistent output but weak style, showing consistency here comes from the shared representation rather than the stylizer.
experiment: Single-stage (one iteration) vs alternating training; qualitative.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 10)
direct_conclusion: The representation enforces consistency even from inconsistent targets; style fidelity requires iterating.
author_hypothesis: Bootstrapping stylization on NeRF outputs makes per-view stylizations progressively more consistent.
confounders: No quantitative consistency/style numbers for this ablation.
anchor: naively training a scene function using a set of inconsistent stylized images leads to cross-view consistent results

claim: Nothing style-specific is reusable: each scene is stylized independently and a new style requires restarting optimisation; total training takes days.
experiment: Reported compute: single V100; T=5 iterations of 500-step per-image stylization + 50k/100k NeRF steps.
measured_outcome: Training (including original NeRF) 3-5 days; rendering 1008x548 image 55 seconds.
direct_conclusion: Per-(scene, style) acquired state; cost dominated by NeRF retraining.
author_hypothesis: Could be combined with arbitrary style transfer or baked for real-time rendering.
confounders: Times include photorealistic NeRF training; not broken down per style.
anchor: we currently stylize each scene independently, and cannot apply an arbitrary style to each scene without restarting the optimization

claim: Adding layer routing (DCM), then paired non-reconstructive training (STRE, SERE), raises text alignment from 0.148 to 0.289 while style similarity falls from 0.274 to 0.224. Leakage removal and style weakening cannot be told apart with these metrics.
experiment: Incremental ablation on 32 styles x 35 prompts, 50k iterations each. Baseline = Q-Former features into all cross-attention layers, reconstruction training. Then +DCM, +STRE, +SERE, full DEADiff. Metrics: CLIP-Interrogator-based style similarity, CLIP text alignment. Fig. 6 qualitative.
measured_outcome: Table 2 (Style Similarity / Text Alignment): Baseline 0.274 / 0.148; +DCM 0.259 / 0.224; +STRE 0.222 / 0.286; +SERE 0.221 / 0.287; DEADiff 0.224 / 0.289. Fig. 6: with STRE, the reference content 'immediately disappears'.
direct_conclusion: Routing alone (DCM) recovers part of text control, and paired training recovers most of it. Each step that reduces visible reference semantics also lowers measured style similarity. That pattern fits both leakage removal and partial style dilution.
author_hypothesis: Reconstruction training brings in reference semantics. DCM reduces them structurally, and STRE makes the Q-Former focus on style. Adding SERE together with reconstruction makes the two representations complementary.
confounders: The SS metric may still reward reference reorganization (the authors concede this for the adapters). Ablations ran 50k iterations vs 100k for the final model. Leakage is assessed only visually. Single-seed numbers with no variance reported.
anchor: Hence, the content of the reference image immediately disappears from the generated results

claim: For T2I-Adapter, lowering the condition weight trades style for text along a curve. At weight 1.0 the output is described as a reorganization of the reference. DEADiff lies off this curve on the reported metric pair.
experiment: Supplement Table 3: T2I-Adapter at image-condition weights 1.0/0.9/0.8 vs DEADiff and other baselines on the same evaluation set (SS, IQ, TA). Fig. 11 trade-off plot.
direct_conclusion: Strength scaling of a CLIP-feature adapter does not remove leakage selectively: lowering the weight weakens style as fast as it restores text. A changed representation and binding (DEADiff) reaches a better SS-TA pair than any of the three weights tested.
confounders: Only three weights were tested. Both metrics are CLIP-based proxies. 'Reorganization of the reference' is a qualitative label, not a measured leakage rate. T2I-Adapter 0.8 has higher TA (0.287) than DEADiff (0.284).
anchor: the generated image essentially becomes a reorganization of the reference image

claim: The 'same-style' training pairs are two Midjourney images generated from the SAME prompt, so they share subject as well as style. Disentanglement therefore comes from captions and layer routing, not from pairs that differ in content.
experiment: Paired dataset construction: about 12,000 subject words x about 14 of 700 style words each gives over 160k prompts and 1.06M Midjourney images. STRE pairs = two images of the same prompt (over 160k items). SERE pairs = same subject word, different style words (1.06M items).
measured_outcome: no outcome measured; dataset statistics only.
direct_conclusion: The style Q-Former's target shares the reference's subject, so the loss does not directly penalize copying the subject. Only the target caption (which describes content) and fine-layer-only injection push toward style-only features. 'Style' is defined by prompt style words (including shots, resolutions, visual angles).
author_hypothesis: The authors chose same-prompt pairs because images with the same style words but different subjects differed too much in style.
confounders: Synthetic, Midjourney-defined style. Style words include camera/viewpoint attributes that overlap with layout. No ablation using cross-subject style pairs.
anchor: for the style representation learning task, we use two distinct images synthesized with the same prompt

claim: DEADiff's style-similarity metric tries to remove content by filtering content words from CLIP-Interrogator prompts. The authors still attribute the adapters' high style scores to reorganizing the reference, so the metric remains leakage-sensitive.
experiment: 32 reference styles (WikiArt, Civitai) x 35 prompts. SS (content-filtered CLIP Interrogator prompt vs image), IQ (LAION aesthetics), TA (CLIP text-image). User study: 18 references, 21 prompts, 24 users, 2016 votes.
measured_outcome: Table 1 (SS / IQ / TA): InST 0.215 / 5.148 / 0.237; CAST 0.224 / 4.922 / 0.282; StyTr2 0.214 / 5.037 / 0.282; T2I-Adapter 0.241 / 5.500 / 0.224; IP-Adapter 0.274 / 5.598 / 0.155; DEADiff 0.229 / 5.840 / 0.284. Overall user preference % (Table 4): InST 6.3, CAST 8.7, StyTr2 13.1, T2I-Adapter 2.7, DEADiff 69.0 (IP-Adapter not in user study).
direct_conclusion: The highest SS goes with the lowest TA (IP-Adapter). DEADiff is best on SS only after excluding the two adapters. The content-filtered SS metric does not cancel reference reorganization.
author_hypothesis: The adapters' high SS comes from their outputs being reorganizations of the reference images.
confounders: The content filtering of interrogator prompts is manual or unspecified. IP-Adapter and T2I-Adapter were run without weight tuning in Table 1 but with it in Fig. 4. CAST and StyTr2 operate on SD-generated content images (different task).
locator: Sec. 4.1; Sec. 4.2; Table 1; Supplement Sec. 6.1-6.2; Table 4
anchor: we filter out the prompts related to the content of the reference image and compute the cosine similarity

claim: Flow-warped initialization plus masked temporal loss reduces short-term (adjacent-frame) warping error on Sintel vs independent per-frame optimization by roughly an order of magnitude.
experiment: 5 MPI Sintel scenes (20-50 frames, 1024x436), 6 paintings; compared temporal loss with DeepFlow or EpicFlow vs no temporal loss with init random / init previous / init previous warped (DeepFlow). Metric: MSE between stylized frame i warped back with GT flow and stylized frame i-1, in non-disoccluded regions (GT occlusions), averaged over 6 styles.
measured_outcome: MSE (pixel values in [0,1]) per scene alley_2/ambush_5/ambush_6/bandage_2/market_6: DeepFlow 0.00061/0.0062/0.012/0.00084/0.0035; EpicFlow 0.00073/0.0068/0.014/0.00080/0.0032; Init prev warped 0.0016/0.0063/0.012/0.0015/0.0049; Init prev 0.010/0.018/0.028/0.0041/0.014; Init random 0.019/0.027/0.037/0.018/0.023 (table printed as 'Table 1', referred to as Table 2 in text).
direct_conclusion: Adjacent-frame consistency along GT flow in visible regions improves with flow-based initialization and temporal loss; on ambush_5/6 the temporal loss gives no gain over warped initialization alone (0.0062 vs 0.0063; 0.012 vs 0.012).
author_hypothesis: Ambush exceptions arise because very large motion makes estimated flow erroneous and impairs the temporal constraint.
confounders: No style-fidelity or style-loss value reported alongside MSE, so a weaker/blurrier stylization could also lower MSE; only 5 short scenes; MSE averaged over 6 styles without variance; weights changed for benchmark (alpha=1, beta=100, gamma=400).
anchor: We warped each stylized frame i back with the ground truth flow and computed the difference

claim: Evaluation correspondence (Sintel GT flow and GT occlusions) differs from the correspondence used by the method (DeepFlow/EpicFlow estimated flow with forward-backward occlusion check).
experiment: Comparison of method description (Sec. 4.1-4.2) with evaluation protocol (Sec. 5.2).
measured_outcome: Method uses DeepFlow or EpicFlow on input frames; disocclusion via forward-backward consistency inequality (5) and motion boundaries via (6). Metric uses Sintel ground-truth optical flow and ground-truth occlusion areas.
direct_conclusion: The metric is not simply re-measuring the estimator the method optimizes against, which strengthens the short-term result; DeepFlow (weaker on Sintel benchmark) scored slightly better than EpicFlow, so flow-benchmark accuracy did not rank the consistency results.
confounders: Both are per-pixel brightness-constancy-along-flow measures; agreement in the type of constraint (warped pixel equality) still favours methods that optimize exactly that quantity.
anchor: The Sintel dataset provides ground truth optical flow and ground truth occlusion areas

claim: Long-term consistency (reappearance after occlusion) and the multi-pass algorithm are not quantitatively evaluated; support is qualitative only.
experiment: Miss Marple scenes: short-term only vs long-term with J={1,10,20,40} (Fig. 3); default vs multi-pass under fast camera motion (Fig. 4); naive c vs c_long weighting shown only in supplementary video.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only; authors state the short-term benchmark cannot evaluate long-term consistency because long-term ground-truth flow is unavailable.
direct_conclusion: Displayed examples show the background keeps its appearance after a person passes when using the long-term loss; no measurement of reappearance consistency or long-horizon drift.
author_hypothesis: Long-term motion estimates enforce consistency of synthesized frames before and after occlusion; multi-pass avoids boundary artifacts propagating into the image.
confounders: Selected scenes; no metric; long-range flow is noted to be more erroneous.
anchor: cannot evaluate the long-term consistency of videos (since we do not have long-term ground truth flow available)

claim: The temporal constraint inherits optical-flow errors; the optimization only partially repairs regions with wrong flow.
experiment: Sintel example showing flow error region vs disocclusion region with flow-uncertainty map (Fig. 7); absolute vs squared temporal error examples (Fig. 6).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Where estimated flow is wrong (sword tip), the masked temporal loss propagates errors that optimization cannot fully recover; the mechanism constrains only what the estimated flow covers.
author_hypothesis: Result quality strongly depends on optical flow quality.
confounders: Single illustrative scenes.
anchor: The quality of results produced by our algorithm strongly depends on the quality of optical flow estimation

claim: No reusable state across frames or videos: every frame requires a new optimization and flow computation; warm-start from warped previous frame only reduces per-frame iterations.
experiment: Runtime reported on Nvidia Titan X at 1024x436.
measured_outcome: Random init, 0.1% threshold: roughly 8-10 min per frame; warped init + temporal loss: about 3 min per frame (2-3x faster); optical flow on CPU about 3 min per frame pair; multi-pass needs at least 10 passes of 100 iterations.
direct_conclusion: Per-content (per-frame) cost dominates; the only reuse is warm-starting from the neighbouring stylized frame.
confounders: Different convergence thresholds between benchmark (0.01%) and runtime figures (0.1%).
anchor: the optimization converges 2 to 3 times faster, three minutes on average

claim: Composition of two reusable LoRAs is not free: ZipLoRA needs a pair-specific optimisation whose cost and storage the paper reports against joint-training and multi-concept baselines.
experiment: Runtime/memory/storage comparison on a single NVIDIA A100: ZipLoRA vs Joint Training (JT), Custom Diffusion (CD), Mix-of-Show (MoS).
measured_outcome: Runtime: ZipLoRA 560 s; JT 3540 s; CD 3890 s; MoS 4980 s (1600 s per ED-LoRA + 1780 s merge). Trainable params 1.6M (ZipLoRA) vs 180M (competitors); GPU memory 21GB vs 38GB; storage 6.5MB merger vectors vs 360MB LoRA.
direct_conclusion: The merge step itself is cheaper than retraining jointly, but it is an additional per-pair acquisition cost on top of the two independently trained LoRAs.
author_hypothesis: ZipLoRA is 'cheap' and hyperparameter-free, suitable for banks of shared subject/style LoRAs.
confounders: Not stated whether 560 s includes training the two base LoRAs (MoS total explicitly includes ED-LoRA training); the 6.5MB storage excludes the two base LoRAs that must still be stored; single-GPU timing without variance.
anchor: while JT and CD takes 3540s and 3890s respectively

claim: Naive weight addition of subject and style LoRAs causes interference that shows mostly as subject-fidelity loss, not as lower CLIP style alignment.
experiment: Alignment scores averaged over 4 subjects x 8 styles: CLIP-I to style reference (style), DINO to subject references (subject), CLIP-T to prompt (text). Compared: ZipLoRA, Joint Training, Direct Merge (w_c=w_s=1), StyleDrop+DreamBooth, Mix of Show, Custom Diffusion. Plus pairwise user study (45 users, 360 responses per comparison).
measured_outcome: Table 2 (style/subject/text): ZipLoRA 0.699/0.420/0.303; Joint Training 0.680/0.378/0.296; Direct Merge 0.702/0.357/0.275; StyleDrop+DreamBooth 0.646/0.394/0.263; Mix of Show 0.635/0.374/0.251; Custom Diffusion 0.616/0.346/0.262 (column order reconstructed from pdftotext; consistent with the text's statement that style alignment is 'competitive' with direct merge). Table 1 user preference for ZipLoRA over Direct Merge 82.7% (other entries' column mapping partly garbled: 71.1%, 68.0%, 87.3%, 88.1%).
direct_conclusion: Direct merge has the highest CLIP-I style score but the lowest subject DINO score among merge-type methods; the interference measured by these proxies is primarily loss of subject identity.
author_hypothesis: Highly aligned LoRA columns superimpose information and degrade the merge; orthogonalising columns avoids this (shown only via a per-layer cosine plot for one pair, Fig. 3b).
confounders: Direct merge only at w_c=w_s=1 (no tuned-coefficient baseline); CLIP-I style metric admitted by the authors to be entangled with semantics; small evaluation set (4 subjects, 8 styles); StyleDrop results obtained from its authors on a different backbone (Muse).
anchor: calculate averages over 4 subjects in 8 styles each

claim: Reference-content leakage acquired in the single-image style LoRA persists through ZipLoRA merging; changing the merge/binding does not remove it.
experiment: Failure-case figure: watercolor style reference containing a cliff, merged with subject LoRAs.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (cliff appears in background of all stylizations)
direct_conclusion: Leakage originates in what the style LoRA retained during acquisition; the merge stage cannot separate it.
author_hypothesis: SDXL style-tuning sometimes captures the subject of the style image as well as its style.
confounders: Single illustrated example; frequency of the failure not quantified.
anchor: SDXL style-tuning fails to disentangle the cliff from the watercolor painting style
review_note: Main reader: leakage acquired during single-image fitting persists through merging; counterexample to binding-only control of leakage.

claim: Single-image style-asset quality is backbone dependent (SDXL vs SDv1.5); assets are refit per backbone and no cross-checkpoint reuse is tested.
experiment: Style-tuning with DreamBooth-LoRA on a single exemplar on SDXL vs SDv1.5 (Fig. 9); ZipLoRA repeated on SDv1.5 with SDv1.5 LoRAs (Fig. 11, Table 3).
measured_outcome: Fig. 9 qualitative only. Table 3 (SDv1.5): ZipLoRA style/subject/text 0.651/0.413/0.283; StyleDrop+DreamBooth (on Muse) 0.646/0.394/0.263; remaining SDv1.5 baseline columns TABLE_TEXT_GARBLED.
direct_conclusion: The same acquisition protocol yields weaker style assets on SDv1.5; the method's merging is re-run with backbone-specific LoRAs rather than transferring assets.
author_hypothesis: Why SDXL learns style from one image better is left open (training data, architecture, training scheme).
confounders: No numbers for style-tuning quality itself; baseline column mapping in Table 3 garbled; StyleDrop compared on a different backbone.
locator: Section 4.1; Appendix B; Fig. 9; Fig. 11; Table 3
anchor: Notice that SDv1.5 (bottom row) fails to capture the reference style consistently.

claim: Iterative training reduces displayed content leakage; the reported style-score drop is uninterpretable because the authors state their style metric favours leakage.
experiment: Feedback-signal ablation: Round 1 vs IT with random selection, CLIP feedback, human feedback; 30 prompts x 64 samples pool; CLIP Text and Style scores; qualitative 'a banana'/'a bottle' in 3d rendering style.
measured_outcome: Text score (a) R1 0.303, (b) Random 0.322, (c) CLIP 0.339, (d) Human 0.328; Style score (a) 0.560, (b) 0.567, (c) 0.542, (d) 0.549. Main Table 2 (6 styles, 190 Parti prompts, 1520 images): Muse 0.323/0.556, R1 0.313/0.705, HF 0.322/0.694, CF 0.329/0.673, Random 0.316/0.678 (Text/Style).
direct_conclusion: Iterative training reduced displayed concept leakage and raised the text score (0.303 -> 0.328 with human feedback). The concurrent style-score change (0.560 -> 0.549) cannot be read as style dilution, because the authors state that their image-similarity style score favours content leakage.
author_hypothesis: The style score favours content leakage (it measures similarity to the style image), so its decrease is partly misleading.
confounders: No leakage-specific metric; CLIP style score conflates leaked content and style; human selection bias; only 6 styles in quantitative evaluation.
anchor: The reduction in concept leakage could be verified with the Text score
review_note: Main reader: authors explicitly say the style score favours leakage (Sec. 4.4.3); agent wording implied dilution.

claim: Content leakage in StyleDrop depends on the sampling operating point (adapter-guidance scale lambda_A, text-guidance lambda_B), not only on the learned representation.
experiment: CFG sweep on StyleDrop R1 and HF models: lambda_A in {0,...,5} with lambda_B=5; lambda_B in {0,...,50} with lambda_A=2; prompts 'An Opera house in Sydney', 'A temple'.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only: large lambda_A collapses content to the style reference; small lambda_B collapses to the style reference; large lambda_B overrides learned style toward generic Muse style; HF model is more robust to scale changes.
direct_conclusion: With the same adapter, leakage vs dilution is traded by guidance scales; the round-2 adapter reduces sensitivity.
author_hypothesis: lambda_A controls style adaptation and lambda_B controls text fidelity; fixing lambda_B=5 and tuning lambda_A is sufficient.
confounders: Qualitative, two prompts; per-style tuning of lambda_A (0.0-2.0 for round 1) means main comparisons may run at different operating points.
locator: Appendix B.3.1; Fig. S4; Table S3
anchor: making the content of synthesized images collapsed to that of the style reference image

claim: Acquiring a StyleDrop style asset can involve two training rounds plus a human/CLIP selection step; only partial cost figures are reported.
experiment: Reported training configuration (Table S3) and human-feedback time.
measured_outcome: 1000 steps per round, lr 0.00003 (base), batch 8 (1 per TPU v3 core); adapter params 0.23M (base round 1), 12.6M (base round 2), 6.3M (super-res); human selection of ~10 images 'about 3 minutes per style'. Wall-clock training time not reported.
direct_conclusion: The default StyleDrop asset is the round-2 adapter (trained on synthetic images with human feedback), so per-style acquisition includes a human-in-the-loop step.
author_hypothesis: StyleDrop can also be optimised on a single A100 with batch size 1.
confounders: No GPU-time measurement; super-resolution adapter adds another fit.
locator: Section 3.3; Section 4.1; Appendix B.1.2; Table S3
anchor: selecting less than a dozen images is enough for IT, and it only takes about 3 minutes per style

claim: Effectiveness of the fitted style asset is strongly backbone dependent (Muse vs Imagen), even with the same training data and text encoder.
experiment: Control experiments: rare token vs descriptive style descriptor; single image vs 10 human-selected synthetic images; Muse adapter tuning vs DreamBooth on Imagen ('melting golden 3d rendering' style).
measured_outcome: qualitative figures (Fig. 6, Fig. 7); Table 2 Style score: DreamBooth on Imagen 0.644 vs StyleDrop HF 0.694 (Imagen prompt-only 0.569, Muse prompt-only 0.556).
direct_conclusion: Imagen needed 10 images and a descriptive descriptor to capture the style, whereas Muse adapters captured it from one image with a rare token.
author_hypothesis: Muse has 'extraordinary fine-tuning data efficiency'; superiority over diffusion models is 'by no means conclusive'.
confounders: Different fine-tuning methods (adapter vs DreamBooth full fine-tune, 300 steps after grid search for Imagen); single style in ablation.
anchor: This suggests that the superiority of StyleDrop on Muse may be coming from its extraordinary fine-tuning data efficiency.

claim: Independently trained style and object adapters are composed at sampling time by logit mixing, without joint training, but interference is not measured and gamma is hand-set.
experiment: 'My object in my style': object adapters from 5-6 DreamBooth images, style adapters from Sec. 4.2 unchanged, gamma in 0.5-0.7; compared with object-only and style-only adapters (teapot, vase, dog).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 5)
direct_conclusion: Style adapters are reusable for composition without retraining; quality depends on a manually chosen gamma.
author_hypothesis: Not requiring joint training gives greater compositional power with pre-trained adapters.
confounders: No quantitative identity or style metric; cherry-picking possible; ZipLoRA later reports StyleDrop+DreamBooth also needs weight adjustment.
anchor: Style adapters from Sec. 4.2 are used without any modification.

claim: No temporal or multi-view consistency metric is reported; the only quantitative metric is LPIPS between rendered frames/depths and the style image over 120 spatio-temporal novel views.
experiment: Following Ref-NPR's benchmark: RGB LPIPS (render vs style image) and Depth LPIPS (rendered depth vs style depth), 120 novel views varying in space and time, NV3D and D-NeRF, vs ARF*, Ref-NPR* (re-implemented for dynamic scenes) and S-DyRF.
direct_conclusion: GAS-NeRF has the lowest depth-to-style LPIPS (baselines identical since geometry unchanged); on RGB LPIPS S-DyRF (NV3D) and ARF* (D-NeRF) are lower than GAS-NeRF, contrary to the text's claim of best scores across all evaluations.
author_hypothesis: Geometry transfer makes results adhere more to the style image.
confounders: Style-similarity LPIPS is a fidelity proxy that rewards style-image resemblance, not consistency; baselines re-implemented by authors; differences small; bold/underline markers lost in text extraction.
anchor: The final score was computed by generating 120 novel views of the stylized dynamic scene, varying over the spatio-temporal domain

claim: Temporal consistency claims (S-DyRF flickers; GAS-NeRF coherent) rest on qualitative figures, supplementary videos and a user study that asks about appearance and geometry, not consistency.
experiment: Qualitative comparison (Fig. 4) and user study with 31 users choosing best method for appearance and geometry on rendered videos.
measured_outcome: User preference: GAS-NeRF 41%, Ref-NPR* 35%, ARF* 19%, S-DyRF 5% (column order as printed). Flicker statement qualitative only.
direct_conclusion: No controlled evidence separates temporal from multi-view consistency or measures either.
author_hypothesis: S-DyRF suffers flickering along the temporal domain.
confounders: User-study criterion mixes appearance and geometry; small sample; no consistency question.
anchor: S-DyRF in particular, suffers from temporal consistency, i.e. has visible flickering effects

claim: Stylization intentionally alters geometry; without regularisation it breaks structure (detached hand) and introduces floaters, shown only qualitatively, and geometric fidelity to the original scene is not measured.
experiment: Ablations: with vs without linear gradient scaling (Fig. 5); with vs without TV and depth-content losses (Fig. 6).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only: floaters near camera without gradient scaling; hand detached from body without L_tv and L_content.
direct_conclusion: Geometry-changing stylization can damage spatio-temporal structural integrity; regularisers reduce visible artifacts in shown examples.
author_hypothesis: Near-camera gradient imbalance causes floaters; quadratic scaling suppresses depth detail too much.
confounders: No quantitative structural or temporal metric; single examples.
anchor: where the hand appears detached from the body

claim: Style state is a per-(scene, style) optimised 4D field; authors identify per-style optimisation as an open limitation.
experiment: Method and conclusion; iteration counts (1000 depth + 600 colour) reported, no wall-clock.
measured_outcome: Iteration counts only; no timing.
direct_conclusion: Nothing style-specific is reusable across styles or scenes.
author_hypothesis: A deep network could provide test-time stylization without optimisation.
anchor: the use of a deep neural network to obtain test-time stylization without the need for computing an optimization for each given style image

claim: The acquired style state is a fine-tuned generator that is reusable across motion-latent sequences because the mapping network and coarse/middle blocks are frozen, preserving the W distribution the motion generator targets.
experiment: Method design; Fig. 5 and Fig. 8 qualitative style-transferred videos (MegaCartoon etc.).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Reuse of the motion generator with a new style depends on keeping the latent space fixed; the compatibility domain of the style asset is the parent StyleGAN checkpoint.
author_hypothesis: Freezing low-resolution blocks 'maintains the distribution of the W space' (asserted, not measured).
confounders: Face-domain data; identity/perceptual regularisation toward the original generator.
anchor: while keeping the mapping network and low-resolution (⩽ 322 , coarse and middle layers in [25]) synthesis blocks fixed

claim: Authors describe the fine-tuned image generator as plug-and-play on any StyleInV motion generator built on the same pretrained StyleGAN, i.e. portability is bounded to the parent checkpoint.
experiment: Fig. 5 caption / Section 3.5 description.
measured_outcome: qualitative statement only
direct_conclusion: Compatibility domain = latent space of the parent generator.
confounders: No cross-checkpoint test.
anchor: the finetuning-based style transfer is “plug-and-play” as the

claim: Temporal consistency of style-transferred videos is inherited from the shared latent trajectory and is shown only qualitatively; reported FID/FVD evaluate unconditional generation, not stylized-video consistency.
experiment: Table 1 FID/FVD on unconditional generation datasets; Fig. 8 style transfer examples.
measured_outcome: No quantitative metric for stylized videos.
direct_conclusion: No measured temporal consistency for the style-transfer variant.
author_hypothesis: The style-transferred video maintains motion of the original (qualitative).
anchor: Table 1: FID, FVD16 and FVD128 results of video generation methods on (a) DeeperForensics

claim: Adding spatial constraints (ControlNet) to a reference-conditioned stylizer reduces style strength: a structure-vs-style trade-off where content-distortion reduction comes with style dilution.
experiment: Preliminary observation motivating the method; no controlled numeric experiment reported.
measured_outcome: no figure or number directly tied to this statement; observation only
direct_conclusion: The authors report observing that ControlNet integration diminishes style strength; no measurement supports magnitude or frequency.
author_hypothesis: A trade-off between spatial structure and stylistic effect is pronounced in current stylization methods.
confounders: No metric, no ControlNet conditioning-scale sweep, no number of examples.
anchor: the direct integration of such a module into the generation process can diminish the style strength

claim: Ablation over content-preservation modules: ControlNet sets global structure, inverted content latent retains finer detail, tile beats canny ControlNet, semantic adapter adds little given a detailed caption, CSD guidance strengthens style.
experiment: Incremental addition of ICL, Canny vs Tile ControlNet, semantic adapter (Sem) and style guidance (SG) to InstantStyle on SDXL; qualitative grid; number of style/content pairs not stated.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 4)
direct_conclusion: In displayed examples, target-content distortion decreases with tile ControlNet + inversion, and CSD guidance compensates style weakening; no quantification.
author_hypothesis: Caching intermediate content features (as in StyleID) may be superfluous given tile ControlNet + inversion; StyleID's initial-latent AdaIN has trivial contribution.
confounders: No metrics at all (no CSD/CLIP/LPIPS/user study); module strengths not reported; cherry-picking possible; content leakage from the style reference not evaluated.
anchor: ControlNet is paramount in defining the overall structural framework, while the initial content latent plays a crucial role

claim: Inversion alone preserves layout but still causes semantic drift of target content (e.g., gender, identity, background), i.e. target-content distortion persists even with content-initialised latents.
experiment: Observation from preliminary experiments with ReNoise/DDIM inversion on human-centred images; not quantified.
measured_outcome: qualitative statement only
direct_conclusion: Target-identity/semantic distortion is a distinct failure from layout distortion in this pipeline; magnitude not measured.
author_hypothesis: A global semantic adapter on the content image mitigates semantic drift when text is absent or insufficient.
confounders: No identity metric; the semantic adapter itself injects content-image CLIP tokens into all blocks, which could also counteract style (not tested).
anchor: inversion alone will still lead to some semantic drift, such as changes in character gender

claim: Prevention of reference-content leakage is asserted via InstantStyle's block-specific injection but is not measured in this paper; the content-subtraction step is even removed 'for convenience'.
experiment: None; claim inherited from InstantStyle.
measured_outcome: none
direct_conclusion: No evidence in this paper about reference-content leakage.
author_hypothesis: Block-specific injection 'effectively prevents content leakage'.
confounders: In image-to-image mode the tile ControlNet and inversion strongly constrain layout, which would mask leakage independently of style routing.
anchor: This approach effectively prevents content leakage and eliminates the need for cumbersome weight tuning processes

claim: Content preservation is bought with per-instance compute: inversion is time-consuming and CSD gradient guidance needs substantial VRAM; costs are stated qualitatively only.
experiment: Limitations statement; no timing or memory numbers.
measured_outcome: no numbers reported
direct_conclusion: Per-content inversion and per-step guidance are non-reusable costs of this pipeline.
anchor: the inversion process proves to be time-consuming, which could be a significant consideration for larger-scale applications

claim: With representation fixed (IP-Adapter CLIP embedding), changing the binding locus (which cross-attention blocks receive image features) changes which reference attributes appear: one block carries colour/material, another spatial layout.
experiment: Per-block injection analysis on IP-Adapter (SDXL); qualitative grid over attention layers.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: For this adapter/backbone, block-restricted injection selects different reference attributes in displayed examples.
author_hypothesis: That two specific layers 'handle style' in general; generality beyond SDXL/IP-Adapter is not tested.
confounders: No metric, no number of references/prompts reported, single backbone; layer roles described subjectively.
anchor: capture style (color, material, atmosphere) and spatial layout (structure, composition) respectively

claim: The paper itself states that whether layout counts as style is reference- and viewer-dependent; layout-block injection is leakage for some references and required style for others.
experiment: Fig. 14 rows 3-4: style-block vs style+layout-block injection on references whose shape/pose may be stylistic.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Leakage labels depend on a declared style scope; the same binding change can be failure or desired transfer.
confounders: Subjective judgement by authors; no annotator protocol.
anchor: As for whether layout is a style, it varies from person to person.

claim: Leakage in the baseline adapter is entangled with strength: authors attribute prior reports of IP-Adapter leakage and weak text control to inappropriate strength settings.
experiment: Strength sweep of IP-Adapter for a style reference (Fig. 4) and weight-tuned comparisons (Fig. 5).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Leakage and style dilution are two ends of a strength axis for this adapter; comparisons at a single fixed strength are not informative about routing.
author_hypothesis: Lower strength solves most problems reported in prior work (asserted, not quantified).
confounders: Per-reference manual tuning; no protocol for choosing strength.
anchor: This can basically be attributed to the same reason, that is, the appropriate strength is not set.

claim: The ablation does not hold the operating point fixed: baseline and subtraction variants are manually strength-tuned while block injection is fixed at 1.0, so the routing benefit is not isolated at matched style strength.
experiment: Fig. 13 subtraction-scale sweep; Fig. 14 baseline / subtraction / style-block / style+layout-block.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only; authors report residual leakage (e.g. flowers on the dog's tail) at reduced baseline strength
direct_conclusion: Subtraction and block selection change displayed leakage; magnitude and matched-strength effect are unmeasured.
author_hypothesis: Style-block-only injection is 'best-performing' (stated as subjective belief).
confounders: Unmatched strength policy; no seeds/prompts count; subjective judgement.
anchor: After applying style block injection, no tuning is adopted anymore, we fix the strength to 1.0.

claim: Restricting injection at inference on a pretrained adapter and training an adapter whose updates are restricted to style blocks gave 'quite similar' results, suggesting the routing locus rather than retraining governs the effect in this setup.
experiment: IP-Adapter (SDXL 1.0) retrained from scratch on 4M text-image pairs updating style blocks only, vs pretrained adapter with other blocks muted.
measured_outcome: qualitative statement, no figure or metric
direct_conclusion: Weak evidence that inference-time routing approximates training-time restriction for this adapter.
confounders: No quantitative comparison shown.
anchor: we find that these two settings achieve quite similar stylized results

claim: Reuse unit is a shared pretrained adapter plus an inference-time block mask; no per-style asset is fitted, but the block identity is a property of the SDXL U-Net and is not shown to transfer to other backbones.
experiment: Method description; all experiments on SDXL.
measured_outcome: n/a
direct_conclusion: Per-style cost is an encoder pass; portability of the routing rule across architectures is untested.
author_hypothesis: Claims to be 'model independent' and applicable to other attention-injection methods; not demonstrated beyond SDXL here.
anchor: There are 11 transformer blocks with SDXL, 4 for downsample blocks, 1 for middle block

claim: CCPL lowers flow-warped temporal loss and inter-frame LPIPS for several architectures, but consistently raises SIFID (weaker style match), showing a consistency-stylization trade-off.
experiment: 10 MPI Sintel clips (50 frames, 12 FPS) x 10 styles; with and without L_ccp on AdaIN, SANet, Linear, SCTNet; SIFID on 100 image pairs; LPIPS between frames and temporal loss (x100) at interval i=1 and i=10.
direct_conclusion: Adding CCPL improves the consistency metrics in all four pairs while every pair's SIFID worsens (by 0.09-0.20), so part of the consistency gain coincides with reduced style-distribution match.
author_hypothesis: CCPL preserves content coherence 'without degrading stylization'; SIFID decrease is described as minor.
confounders: SIFID computed on 10x10 images, not on the video frames; human preference mixes quality, style and consistency; no occlusion masking stated for the warped temporal loss.
locator: Section 4.1 'Metrics'; Section 4.2 'Video style transfer'; Section 4.4; Table 1
anchor: the proposed CCPL improves the temporal consistency a lot with a minor decrease of the SIFID score

claim: Training uses no temporal correspondence (spatial neighbour patches within one image as a surrogate for motion), while evaluation uses Sintel GT flow for adjacent frames and PWC-Net flow for 9-frame gaps.
experiment: Method: CCPL on single images, with assumption that difference between nearby patches approximates same-location difference across adjacent frames for small Delta t. Evaluation: temporal loss from Wang et al. (ReReVST) warping one stylized frame with optical flow.
measured_outcome: Short-term: ground-truth optical flow from MPI Sintel; long-term (9 frames in between): PWC-Net estimated flow; LPIPS between stylized frames has no warping.
direct_conclusion: The evaluation correspondence (dense flow) is of a different type and source than the training signal (spatial-neighbour feature differences); the claimed equivalence of neighbour patches to temporal correspondence is asserted, not tested. Long-term metric depends on an estimator that the method never sees.
author_hypothesis: Global inconsistency is dominated by local inconsistencies; only simple transformations (translation, rotation) occur locally between adjacent frames.
confounders: Occlusion masks not mentioned in the temporal loss; PWC-Net errors at 9-frame gaps unquantified.
anchor: For short-term consistency, we directly use the ground-truth optical flow from the MPI Sintel data-set

claim: More CCPL layers and higher CCPL/style weight ratio increase measured consistency while weakening stylization; the default is a chosen trade-off point.
experiment: Number of CCPL layers 0-4, sampled vectors {16,32,64,128}, loss weight ratio sweep; stylization = SIFID; consistency = 20 - 10 x LPIPS - temporal loss (short- and long-term).
measured_outcome: Fig. 8 curves only (numbers not in text): consistency rises with layers while stylization score falls; 3->4 layers gives minor consistency gain and 'much weaker' stylization; 128 vs 64 vectors close in consistency with style degeneration; ratio 0.5 chosen.
direct_conclusion: The consistency metric can be improved by turning up a regulariser that weakens style; the paper does control for this by reporting SIFID jointly, and its default is a trade-off rather than a free gain.
author_hypothesis: The loss weight ratio is a handle to adjust temporal consistency and stylization.
confounders: Composite consistency score is an ad hoc combination of LPIPS and temporal loss.
anchor: The loss weight ratio can also be regarded as a handle to adjust temporal consistency and stylization

claim: A multi-frame flow-based method (ReReVST) remains best on short-term warped temporal loss and LPIPS; the single-frame CCPL model is better only at i=10 and in SIFID.
experiment: Same Sintel protocol; comparison against ReReVST, MCCNet, AdaAttN, IE, DSTN, Linear, SANet, AdaIN.
measured_outcome: ReReVST SIFID 2.78, LPIPS 0.137/0.359, Temp 2.97/5.19, Pre Art/Vid 0.046/0.062; SCTNet+Lccp SIFID 2.43, LPIPS 0.144/0.367, Temp 3.45/5.08, Pre 0.122/0.138; MCCNet SIFID 2.34, LPIPS 0.162/0.424, Temp 4.21/7.64.
direct_conclusion: Explicit multi-frame coupling still yields lowest adjacent-frame error; CCPL's advantage over ReReVST is on style-distribution match and preference, not short-term consistency.
author_hypothesis: Full model performs on par with the SOTA multi-frame method.
confounders: Official code of each method at default strengths; SIFID on images not videos.
anchor: performs on par with the SOTA multi-frame method: ReReVST [63]. However, our SIFID score exceeds ReReVST

claim: The paper notes that directly matching patch differences would make outputs copy content and erase style; the contrastive form is motivated to avoid this, but the SIFID increase indicates residual dilution.
experiment: Design rationale for InfoNCE over direct difference matching (no direct-matching baseline reported).
measured_outcome: No experiment comparing direct matching vs contrastive; SIFID increases with CCPL (Table 1).
