direct_conclusion: Target-content preservation and style dilution are coupled through this regulariser; the failure the contrastive form is meant to avoid is not measured directly.
author_hypothesis: Contrastive formulation avoids direct contradiction with style losses.
anchor: an easy workaround of the network is to encourage G similar to C, meaning that this constraint would contradict the purpose of style transfer

claim: CAS measures target-content alignment (AdaIN-normalised DINOv2 feature distance between output and content image), not leakage of the style reference's content; low CAS also rewards style dilution.
experiment: Metric definition: CAS_i = || Ada(phi(C)) - Ada(phi(T_i)) ||^2 with phi = DINOv2 image encoder, Ada(F) = (F - mu(F)) / rho(F) (mean/'variance' normalisation following AdaIN); lower is better.
measured_outcome: definition only
direct_conclusion: CAS quantifies target-content distortion relative to the content image after removing channel statistics; it contains no term comparing the output with the style reference, so reference-content leakage is not measured.
author_hypothesis: Normalisation removes 'style information' so CAS captures content only; DINOv2 chosen as closest to human filtering (no numbers given).
confounders: The same CAS was used to select training targets (min-CAS candidate) and then as the evaluation metric, so CSGO is trained toward the evaluation metric; AdaIN normalisation removes only first/second-order statistics, not texture.
anchor: the feature distance between the content semantic features (without style information) of the generated image

claim: Quantitative trade-off: methods with lowest content distortion (StyleID) have the weakest style score, while CSGO reports both the highest CSD and second-lowest CAS on its own test set.
experiment: IMAGStyle test set: 248 content images x 206 style images; CSD (style similarity to reference, higher better) and CAS (lower better); baselines StyTR2, Style-Aligned, StyleID, InstantStyle, StyleShot, StyleShot-lineart.
measured_outcome: Table 1 (CSD / CAS): StyTR2 0.2695 / 0.9699; Style-Aligned 0.4274 / 1.3930; StyleID 0.0992 / 0.4873; InstantStyle 0.3175 / 1.3147; StyleShot 0.4522 / 1.5105; StyleShot-lineart 0.3903 / 1.0750; CSGO 0.5146 / 0.8386 (mapping by column order).
direct_conclusion: On this benchmark, StyleID preserves content most (CAS 0.4873) with very low CSD (0.0992); CSGO attains the highest CSD with CAS below all baselines except StyleID.
author_hypothesis: Decoupled, explicit content/style injection explains the gain.
confounders: Test set and CAS both from the authors; CSGO trained on CAS-selected targets; operating points (delta_c=0.5, lambda_s=1.0) tuned by authors while baselines use defaults; text claims Style-Aligned has very low CAS and low CSD, which conflicts with the order-mapped values (0.4274 / 1.3930), so the mapping or the text is unreliable for Style-Aligned.
anchor: maintain the original content too strongly in sketch style transfer scenarios (CAS is very low)

claim: Content-scale and style-scale sweeps show style dilution as content binding strengthens: large ControlNet weight delta_c severely weakens style; lambda_s < 1.0 also weakens style.
experiment: Sweep delta_c in {0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9,1.2}, CFG in {1,10,20}, lambda_s in {0.5,1.0,1.5}, lambda_c in {0.1,1.0} on example content/style pairs.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 13)
direct_conclusion: In displayed examples the content-preservation/style-strength balance is set by scalar weights; content fidelity rises and style weakens with delta_c.
confounders: Two example pairs; no metrics per setting; recommended defaults chosen visually.
anchor: when δc is large (e.g., 0.9 and 1.2), the style information is severely weakened

claim: Leakage runs in both directions: authors report that ControlNet content injection leaks the content image's style (diluting target style) and add style injection into the ControlNet branch to counter it.
experiment: (1) without ControlNet content control; (2) with content control but no style injection into ControlNet; (3) full model; qualitative.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 9, Fig. 12)
direct_conclusion: Removing style injection in the ControlNet branch visibly weakens style in displayed examples; ControlNet improves layout retention.
author_hypothesis: ControlNet injection 'may leak style information of the content image C'.
confounders: No metric; few examples.
anchor: ControlNet injections in the content control may leak style information of the content image C

claim: Reference-content leakage reduction is asserted (Resampler projection, explicit decoupling, text-driven results obeying prompts) but only shown qualitatively; no leakage metric is reported.
experiment: Linear vs Perceiver-Resampler style projection (Fig. 10); style token number t in {4,12,16,32} (Fig. 11); text-driven comparison vs InstantStyle, StyleShot, StyleAligned, DEADiff (Fig. 6).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Displayed examples suggest the Resampler projection avoids content leakage and more tokens strengthen style; whether more tokens also increase reference-content leakage is not examined.
author_hypothesis: Explicit decoupling means 'style images only inject style information without exposing content'.
confounders: Training targets come from B-LoRA recombination whose style LoRA may itself carry reference content; no text-alignment or leakage metric for text-driven mode.
anchor: Using the Resampler structure captures more detailed style features while avoiding content leakage

claim: Feed-forward reuse is purchased by shifting per-style fitting into dataset construction: one B-LoRA per content and per style image, then automatic CAS filtering.
experiment: Pipeline description: 11,000 content and 10,000 style LoRAs (rank 64, 1000 steps each); model trained 80,000 steps on 8 H800 GPUs.
measured_outcome: Training setup numbers only; no inference-time or cost comparison reported.
direct_conclusion: Inference needs no per-style optimisation; the paper does not report the dataset-construction compute or inference speed relative to inversion baselines.
author_hypothesis: Inversion-based baselines significantly increase inference time (not measured).
confounders: Implicit B-LoRA separation is stated to be unstable (Fig. 2 failure cases).
anchor: the implicit separate approach is unstable, resulting in the content and style LoRA

claim: IP-Adapter's training objective and headline metric reward reproducing the reference image as a whole (content and style); it does not separate style from reference content, so leakage is the designed behaviour, not a measured failure.
experiment: COCO2017 val, 5,000 image prompts x 4 samples = 20,000 images per method; CLIP-I = CLIP ViT-L/14 image-embedding similarity between generated image and image prompt; CLIP-T = CLIPScore with the image prompt's caption.
measured_outcome: Table 1: IP-Adapter (22M trainable) CLIP-T 0.588, CLIP-I 0.828; SD unCLIP 0.584 / 0.810; SD Image Variations 0.548 / 0.760; Open unCLIP 0.608 / 0.858; T2I-Adapter (Style) 0.485 / 0.648; Uni-ControlNet (Global) 0.506 / 0.736; ControlNet Shuffle 0.421 / 0.616. (Row-to-number mapping reconstructed from garbled column order; consistent with text.)
direct_conclusion: IP-Adapter reproduces the reference's overall CLIP semantics better than other adapters at this operating point (text empty, lambda=1).
author_hypothesis: The global CLIP embedding 'can represent the rich content and style of the image'.
confounders: CLIP-I is a whole-image similarity proxy that cannot distinguish style transfer from content copying; text prompt empty; no style-only metric; baselines use different backbones and training data.
anchor: CLIP-I: the similarity in CLIP image embedding of generated images with the image prompt.
review_note: Main reader: that CLIP-I rewards reference reproduction is inferred from the metric definition; only the value 0.828 is measured.

claim: Richer reference representation (fine-grained CLIP grid tokens vs. global embedding) increases fidelity but also transfers the reference's spatial structure, reducing diversity: representation granularity changes retained layout information.
experiment: IP-Adapter with global CLIP embedding (4 tokens) vs. IP-Adapter with 16 learnable query tokens over penultimate-layer CLIP grid features; same binding; qualitative comparison.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 11)
direct_conclusion: In displayed examples, fine-grained features reproduce reference spatial structure more, which the authors frame as reduced diversity.
author_hypothesis: Global embedding 'may lose some information'; fine-grained features 'learn the spatial structure information'; extra text/pose conditions can restore diversity.
confounders: No metric, number of examples not stated, training budget of the variant not stated; not evaluated as a style task.
anchor: it can also learn the spatial structure information, which may reduce the diversity of generated images

claim: Changing binding from concatenation into the frozen text cross-attention to a decoupled image cross-attention increases consistency with the image prompt (i.e., more reference information transferred), shown only qualitatively.
experiment: Simple adapter (image tokens concatenated with text tokens in frozen cross-attention) vs. decoupled IP-Adapter, both trained 200,000 steps with the same configuration; qualitative.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 10)
direct_conclusion: Decoupled binding yields outputs more consistent with the image prompt in displayed examples.
author_hypothesis: Frozen K/V projections trained for text only align image features to text and lose image-specific information, giving only coarse control 'e.g., image style'.
confounders: Qualitative only; 'consistency' conflates content and style; no leakage measurement.
anchor: the IP-Adapter not only can generate higher quality images than the simple adapter, but also can generate more consistent images

claim: Authors state as a limitation that IP-Adapter only produces images resembling the reference in both content and style; the scalar lambda trades image vs. text influence but is not quantified.
experiment: Multimodal prompts on Realistic Vision V4.0 with manually adjusted lambda; conclusion/limitation statement.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 8, Fig. 9); no lambda sweep reported
direct_conclusion: Image-text balance is exposed as a global scalar; the paper offers no measurement of how lambda trades reference content against text adherence.
confounders: lambda chosen per example; cherry-picked best-of-4 in qualitative comparisons (Section 4.2.2).
anchor: it can only generate images that resemble the reference images in content and style

claim: Adapter weights trained once are reusable across community checkpoints fine-tuned from the same base and with structural-control adapters, but portability is bounded to that base-model family.
experiment: Apply SD v1.5-trained IP-Adapter to Realistic Vision V4.0, Anything v4, ReV Animated and SD v1.4; combine with ControlNet / T2I-Adapter without fine-tuning.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Fig. 6)
direct_conclusion: Within the SD v1.x family the adapter transfers without retraining in displayed examples; no cross-architecture test.
author_hypothesis: Freezing the base model is what makes the adapter reusable.
confounders: No quantitative evaluation on custom models; output style mixes with the checkpoint's own style (noted in text).
anchor: once IP-Adapter is trained, it can be directly reusable on custom models fine-tuned from the same base model

claim: Changing the style representation (global projection; prompt-based patch selection) sharply improves text alignment (less reference-content leakage per authors) but lowers CSD style score, so leakage reduction co-occurs with lower measured style similarity.
experiment: Stylized T2V test set: 12 style images x 16 prompts = 192 pairs; variants B1 raw CLIP global embedding, B2 with global projection (GP), B3 all patch features, B4 random selection of same number of patches, B5 prompt-similarity selection, B6 GP + selection; metrics UMT score (text-video alignment) and CSD score (style similarity to reference).
direct_conclusion: GP raises UMT from 0.892 to 2.337 while CSD falls 0.561 -> 0.443; patch selection raises UMT 0.771 -> 2.331 with CSD 0.534 -> 0.452. Random dropping already recovers most text alignment (2.129). Prompt-based vs random selection differ by 0.202 UMT at nearly equal CSD.
author_hypothesis: Raw CLIP embeddings/patches 'invite content leakage'; higher CSD of leaky variants reflects content copying rather than style.
confounders: No direct leakage metric: UMT text alignment is used as an inverse-leakage proxy, and CSD may reward copied content; cannot separate leakage reduction from style dilution with these two metrics; single test set of 12 styles.
anchor: the use of Global Project (GP) can effectively prevent content leakage caused by directly using the CLIP image embedding

claim: Highest CSD style score belongs to the baseline the authors say copies reference content (VideoComposer), with near-zero text alignment, showing CSD style similarity is confounded by reference-content leakage.
experiment: 192 style-prompt pairs; VideoComposer vs StyleCrafter vs StyleMaster; CLIP-Text, UMT, CSD, visual quality, dynamic quality, motion smoothness.
measured_outcome: Table 2 (CLIP-Text / UMT / CSD / VisualQuality / DynamicQuality / MotionSmooth): VideoComposer 0.057 / -2.268 / 0.680 / 2.159 / 2.284 / 0.975; StyleCrafter 0.294 / 1.994 / 0.448 / 2.140 / 2.306 / 0.973; Ours 0.305 / 2.329 / 0.463 / 2.370 / 2.496 / 0.994.
direct_conclusion: VideoComposer's CSD 0.680 coincides with CLIP-Text 0.057 and negative UMT; the authors attribute it to content copying, consistent with CSD rewarding leakage.
author_hypothesis: VideoComposer 'directly copies the content in the reference image, therefore exhibiting a higher style score'.
confounders: Copying judged qualitatively (Fig. 8); different base models across methods.
anchor: it directly copies the content in the reference image, therefore exhibiting a higher style score

claim: Style extent is coupled to a motion module: negative motion-adapter scale increases CSD and dynamics but harms text alignment and smoothness beyond -0.3, an entanglement of style strength with the temporal prior's real-world domain.
experiment: Motion adapter scale alpha in {-1, -0.5, -0.3, -0.1, 0} on the 192-pair test set.
direct_conclusion: CSD rises from 0.443 (alpha=0) to 0.465 (alpha=-1); motion smoothness drops from 0.994 to 0.990 and UMT is best at -0.3. Style strength is modulated by a component not designed to carry style.
author_hypothesis: Because the adapter was trained on real-world still videos, the negative ratio pushes outputs away from the real-world domain, increasing stylisation.
confounders: Small CSD differences; UMT non-monotonic; single seed setting not stated.
anchor: the negative ratio can generate results away from the real-world domain, leading to a more stylistic video

claim: Video consistency is evaluated only with VBench motion smoothness (AMT-based) and dynamic degree (RAFT), plus frame-wise image metrics; no long-range, occlusion, or style-consistency-across-frames measurement, and transfer consistency against the source video is not measured.
experiment: Two-fold video evaluation: frame-by-frame image stylization metrics; motion quality via VBench motion smoothness and dynamic degree; video style transfer compared on 4 internet videos x 16 styles vs DomoAI and InstantStyle+AnyV2V (Table 8).
measured_outcome: Table 2 MotionSmooth: Ours 0.994, StyleCrafter 0.973, VideoComposer 0.975. Table 8 (CSD / CLIP-Text / UMT / Visual / DynamicDegree / MotionSmooth): DomoAI 0.421 / 0.290 / 2.349 / 2.331 / 0.005 / 0.995; InstantStyle&AnyV2V 0.313 / 0.312 / 2.984 / 2.158 / 0.233 / 0.971; Ours 0.434 / 0.319 / 3.311 / 2.400 / 0.082 / 0.989.
direct_conclusion: Smoothness metrics show low local jitter for StyleMaster; in transfer, DomoAI is smoother (0.995) with almost no dynamics (0.005), illustrating that smoothness can be maximised by static output. No metric checks fidelity to source-video motion or long-horizon drift.
confounders: Motion smoothness rewards static videos; dynamic degree rewards motion regardless of source fidelity; only 4 transfer videos; resizing to 512x512 for one baseline.
locator: Section 4 (Evaluation Metrics); Table 2; Supplementary Section 10; Table 8
anchor: we adopt motion smoothness metric and dynamic degree metric proposed in VBench [21] for evaluation

claim: Colour in the tile content condition interferes with style injection (darker outputs); removing colour (gray tile) is the fix: the content channel can leak content-image colour, a reverse-direction factor entanglement.
experiment: ControlNet conditions: Canny vs RGB tile vs gray tile; qualitative.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 10)
direct_conclusion: In displayed examples, RGB tile gives layout but carries colour that competes with reference colour; gray tile avoids this.
confounders: No metric; image-trained ControlNet.
anchor: the color information within the guidance can interrupt the style injection, resulting in darker outputs

claim: In image style transfer, StyleMaster has higher CSD and better ArtFID but worse LPIPS/CFSD than StyleID: stronger style comes with more target-content change on the authors' 96-pair set.
experiment: 8 content x 12 style images = 96 pairs, image treated as one-frame video; CSD, ArtFID, FID, LPIPS, CFSD; StyleID, InstantStyle, CSGO default settings.
direct_conclusion: Ours is best on CSD/ArtFID/FID; StyleID preserves content structure best (CFSD 1.06). CSGO's CFSD (5.12) is the worst here.
author_hypothesis: Some detail loss is an expected transformation for simple line styles.
confounders: Small test set (8 contents); CSD values for StyleID (0.40) and CSGO (0.35) differ greatly from CSGO paper's Table 1 (StyleID 0.0992, CSGO 0.5146), indicating strong protocol dependence of CSD.
anchor: While slightly underperforming in content alignment metrics, we argue that effective style transfer requires balancing style fidelity and content retention

claim: Cross-view consistency follows by construction from one shared radiance field with frozen density and view-dependence removed; style losses are applied only at training viewpoints.
experiment: Method construction (Sec. 4.4): density fixed, only appearance optimised; SH reduced to DC term (Plenoxels) or view directions zeroed (TensoRF); each iteration renders one randomly selected training viewpoint.
measured_outcome: No measurement; design statement only.
direct_conclusion: Geometry is the photorealistic reconstruction's geometry, so any multi-view coherence is inherited from the shared field; the loss itself does not constrain views between or beyond training cameras.
author_hypothesis: NNFM captures local details 'in a view-consistent way' better than global-statistics losses.
confounders: Removing view-dependent appearance trivially reduces view-dependent variation; consistency is a property of the representation, not of the style loss.
anchor: we fix the density component of the initial photorealistic radiance field

claim: ARF reports no quantitative cross-view consistency metric; its user study asks only about style match, so multi-view consistency is asserted via supplementary videos, not measured.
experiment: User study: 25 randomly selected (scene, style) pairs, ~12 ratings each, 2AFC vs Huang et al. and Chiang et al.; question is which stylized video better matches the style image.
measured_outcome: Users preferred ARF over Huang et al. 86.8% and over Chiang et al. 94.1% of the time (style match only).
direct_conclusion: Evidence supports better perceived style match; it does not test temporal/view consistency, occlusion, or held-out views.
author_hypothesis: Consistent results across viewpoints are visible in the supplementary video.
confounders: Baselines use released pre-trained models (feed-forward/hypernetwork) vs ARF's per-style optimisation; no strength matching.
anchor: The user is then asked to select the result that better matches the style of the given style image

claim: Geometric errors of the underlying reconstruction (floaters) propagate into stylized renderings because stylization does not modify or regularise density.
experiment: Stated limitation; no controlled experiment.
measured_outcome: qualitative statement only
direct_conclusion: Shared-representation consistency is only as good as the photorealistic geometry; stylization inherits its artifacts.
author_hypothesis: Floaters could be removed with additional density regularisers.
anchor: geometric artifacts, e.g., floaters, in the radiance fields can cause artifacts

claim: The acquired style state is a per-(scene, style) optimised radiance field; every new style requires minutes of re-optimisation, though rendering afterwards is real-time.
experiment: Reported optimisation time per style image on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090.
measured_outcome: ~3 mins for forward-facing captures, ~20 mins for 360 captures per style image.
direct_conclusion: Reuse is across viewpoints of one scene only; nothing is reused across styles except the photorealistic field and VGG.
confounders: Excludes time to reconstruct the photorealistic field; single GPU type.
anchor: a relatively time-consuming optimization procedure is still required for every style image

claim: Replacing NNFM with a Gram loss yields less faithful, more artifact-laden stylization (a style-dilution contrast), shown only qualitatively.
experiment: Ablation: full pipeline vs no colour transfer vs NNFM->Gram vs NNFM->CNNMRF on example scenes; also VGG block choice (Fig. 9).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Within ARF's pipeline the local NN-matching loss transfers more style detail than global Gram statistics in the shown examples.
author_hypothesis: Gram matrices average out local style details.
confounders: Loss weights not re-tuned per loss; cherry-picked examples; no leakage or content-distortion metric.
anchor: Replacing the NNFM loss with the commonly-used Gram loss [11] leads to less compelling results

claim: InST's style token is a per-painting fitted asset (about 20 minutes per image), reusable across contents and prompts; it is not a feed-forward encoder for unseen styles.
experiment: Implementation details: training time per image; inference same as SDM.
measured_outcome: about 20 minutes per image on one NVIDIA GeForce RTX3090, batch size 1, base lr 0.001; synthesis time 'the same as SDM'.
direct_conclusion: Acquisition is per-style optimisation; inference cost is ordinary SD sampling plus stochastic inversion of the content.
author_hypothesis: The CLIP-initialised attention module makes inversion efficient and accurate.
confounders: Single timing figure; no comparison of wall-clock to textual inversion; whether the module could generalise to unseen paintings without retraining is not evaluated.
anchor: about 20 minutes each image on one NVIDIA GeForce RTX3090 with a batch size of 1

claim: Attention-based inversion converges in about 1000 iterations versus roughly 10x more for textual inversion, a reduction in per-style acquisition steps.
experiment: Optimization-progress comparison with Textual Inversion (500-6000 iterations) on a reference; CLIP-based accuracy/editability table vs TI, SDM caption, MLP and no-dropout ablations.
measured_outcome: Fig. 5 qualitative; Table 1 TABLE_TEXT_GARBLED (values 78.92, 71.03, 80.72, 69.03, 66.99, 68.84, 63.83, 72.25, 66.53 appear without unambiguous column mapping).
direct_conclusion: Iteration count to visually match the reference is lower for InST in the shown example.
author_hypothesis: TI's simple optimisation scheme needs 10x the iterations.
confounders: Single-image qualitative convergence; TI trained on one image (outside its 3-5 image design).
anchor: Our method can quickly optimize to the target text embedding in about 1000 iterations

claim: InST deliberately treats reference semantic elements and object shapes as style, so reference-object transfer is counted as success rather than leakage.
experiment: Qualitative comparison with ArtFlow, AdaAttN, StyleFormer, IEST, StyTr2, CAST (Fig. 4); user study 2,262 votes from 87 participants on artistic consistency.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure (e.g. cars changed to roadsters, stars added, facial forms changed); Table 2 preference values TABLE_TEXT_GARBLED in pairing.
direct_conclusion: The paper's notion of style includes reference semantics; target-content changes are presented as desirable.
author_hypothesis: Artistic style includes high-level attributes such as semantic elements and object shapes.
confounders: User study instructed participants that artistic consistency is the main metric, biasing against content preservation.
anchor: the cars in the content image are changed to roadsters

claim: Without stochastic content inversion, reference semantics overwrite target structure (buildings become trees/mountains); the strength parameter trades this off.
experiment: Ablation of stochastic inversion and strength (0.4, 0.6) on content images (Fig. 8a).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: Target-content distortion depends on the content-binding step (noise initialisation) and the strength operating point.
author_hypothesis: Random noise carries 'detail representation'; predicted noise preserves content semantics.
confounders: Qualitative; no content-preservation metric.
anchor: the buildings in the content images are turned into trees or mountains without stochastic inversion

claim: Colour is not reliably transferred semantically by the token; an external AdaIN tone-transfer module is optionally added, indicating colour-vs-other-factor entanglement.
experiment: Limitation discussion with and without tone transfer (Fig. 9).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only
direct_conclusion: The learned embedding does not control colour correspondence; colour is handled by a separate operator.
author_hypothesis: Users differ on whether content colours should be retained.
confounders: Qualitative only.
anchor: our method may fail to transfer the color in a one-to-one correspondence semantically

claim: Cross-view 'stability' is not numerically discriminated among 3D methods: ARF, SNeRF and Ref-NPR receive identical stability because they share the same fixed density field.
experiment: Table 1 'Stability' row (long-range consistency following SNeRF) reported as a pass/fail mark for Texler, SNeRF, ARF, Ref-NPR.
measured_outcome: TABLE_TEXT_GARBLED for the marks (rendered as '7 3 3 3', apparently fail for Texler, pass for the three 3D methods); caption states methods except Texler get the same stability.
direct_conclusion: Consistency among radiance-field methods is a property of the shared frozen geometry, not a measured advantage of Ref-NPR.
author_hypothesis: Text claims Ref-NPR achieves higher cross-view geometric consistency than state-of-the-art scene stylization.
confounders: SNeRF is re-implemented on Plenoxels; density frozen for all 3D methods so stability is identical by construction.
anchor: Methods except Texler get the same stability as they adopt the same optimized density field

claim: Depth-based ray registration cannot supervise regions occluded in the reference view; occluded regions are filled by semantic feature matching, whose effect is shown only qualitatively.
experiment: Ablations w/o L_ref, reference view only, w/o L_feat (TCM), w/o L_color, and w/ vs w/o TCM; plus smooth-update ablation (Fig. C.4).
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Figs. 6, 7, C.4): w/o L_feat occluded regions become photorealistic; w/o L_color colour mismatch in occluded regions.
direct_conclusion: Geometric correspondence covers only reference-visible surfaces; occluded content relies on semantic (not geometric) correspondence whose correctness is not measured.
author_hypothesis: Semantic correspondence in the scene is consistent before and after stylization.
confounders: No metric for occluded-region plausibility; examples selected.
anchor: it struggles to register reference rays to occluded regions under such a camera

claim: The reference-fidelity metric is computed only on the 10 test views nearest the reference, and the 2D video baseline (Texler) scores slightly better on it.
experiment: Ref-LPIPS between stylized reference and top-10 nearest test novel views on 8 scenes (Synthetic, LLFF, T&T); robustness = PSNR between renders of omega_NP and of NeRFs re-stylized from its own renders.
measured_outcome: Ref-LPIPS avg: Texler 0.335, SNeRF 0.405, ARF 0.394, Ref-NPR 0.339. Robustness PSNR: Texler 18.69, SNeRF 26.03, ARF 26.34, Ref-NPR 28.11. Flower: Texler 0.230 vs Ref-NPR 0.289.
direct_conclusion: Near-reference fidelity is measured; far-from-reference and occluded-region quality is not quantified. Texler wins Ref-LPIPS on average.
author_hypothesis: Texler fails when the camera diverges from the reference pose (shown qualitatively).
confounders: Near-view metric favours propagation methods that are accurate only near the reference; large per-scene variance; robustness test is a self-consistency proxy.
locator: Section 4.3; Table 1; Appendix Table B.1, Fig. B.1
anchor: Texler [38] achieves slightly better reference-related LPIPS scores

claim: Stated failure modes: no meaningful semantic correspondence in the reference, intricate geometric structures, and large scenes with a single reference.
experiment: Failure-case figure.
measured_outcome: qualitative figure only (Fig. 10)
direct_conclusion: Correspondence-based propagation is bounded by reference coverage and matchability.
author_hypothesis: Multiple references mitigate large-scene coverage (Fig. 9).
anchor: it may not perform well when no meaningful semantic correspondence is found in the reference view

claim: Each new stylized reference requires a fresh per-scene optimisation; only content-domain correspondences are cheap one-time precomputation.
experiment: Implementation details and TCM cost report.
measured_outcome: 10 epochs per scene on one NVIDIA 3090 (wall-clock not given); TCM correspondence ~2 seconds for 100 images.
direct_conclusion: Style state is a per-(scene, reference) radiance field; not reusable across styles or scenes.
confounders: No total wall-clock for optimisation reported.
locator: Section 4.1; Appendix C 'Discussion on TCM matching'
anchor: The correspondence is only computed once and costs around 2 seconds for a set with 100 images

claim: CPC metric measures semantic agreement of output with a VLM caption of the content reference (CLIP score), zeroed when CSD to the style reference is below a threshold; it targets content-copy-without-style, not reference-content leakage or structural fidelity.
experiment: Metric definition: CPC@thresh = CLIP(I_res, T_vlm) if CSD(I_res, I_style) >= thresh else 0, with T_vlm a Qwen-VL detailed caption of the content reference; reported at thresh 0.5 and '0.3:0.9'.
measured_outcome: definition only
direct_conclusion: CPC couples content and style: a method can lose CPC either by content change or by style dilution below threshold. Caption-level CLIP cannot detect spatial/structural distortion or identity change not described in the caption, nor objects leaked from the style reference unless they displace captioned content.
author_hypothesis: A model that replicates the content reference without transferring style would otherwise get an artificially high content score.
confounders: CSD itself can be inflated by reference-content leakage (noted in other papers), which would pass the threshold; the meaning of '@0.3:0.9' (presumably averaged over thresholds) is not defined in the text.
anchor: a model that simply replicates the content reference without transferring style would receive an artificially high content score

claim: On the authors' 2,000-pair benchmark TeleStyle leads all baselines in CSD, CPC and aesthetics; no ablation isolates which component causes this.
experiment: 50 style x 40 content references = 2,000 pairs; CSD, CPC@0.5, CPC@0.3:0.9, LAION aesthetic score; baselines StyleID, StyleShot, InstantStyle, CSGO, OmniStyle, OmniGen-v2, DreamO.
direct_conclusion: TeleStyle scores highest on all four metrics on this benchmark. Because CPC is gated by CSD, part of the CPC gap reflects CSD differences.
author_hypothesis: Curriculum continual learning on hybrid clean/noisy triplets yields generalisation without losing content fidelity.
confounders: No ablation of curriculum stages (stage benefits stated as 'validation results demonstrate' without numbers); benchmark and metric designed by authors; baselines on different backbones/resolutions; no leakage metric; StyleID's CSD here (0.453) differs from CSGO paper (0.0992) and StyleMaster paper (0.40), showing protocol sensitivity.
anchor: Our TeleStyle V1 demonstrates significant advantages over previous models

claim: Identity leakage of the SDXL-based style-reference generator (CDST) led the authors to exclude humans from synthetic prompts; noisy synthetic content references cause content degradation, controlled by mixing ratio, not measured.
experiment: Dataset construction choices; no measurement of identity leakage or of degradation with synthetic-only training reported.
measured_outcome: no measurement reported
direct_conclusion: Leakage in the data generator is acknowledged as a data-quality risk and avoided by prompt filtering; its effect on the trained model is not quantified.
author_hypothesis: Training on D_synthetic alone leads to content degradation; a low mixing ratio avoids catastrophic forgetting.
confounders: The 'carefully tuned' ratio is not reported.
anchor: we exclude humans from these prompts, as we observed that SDXL-based CDST suffers from identity leakage

claim: Video temporal treatment relies on a learned temporal prior anchored to a stylized first frame (temporal index 0); no flow, correspondence or consistency metric is used, and no quantitative video evaluation is reported.
experiment: Architecture and training description; qualitative examples only (Fig. 2).
measured_outcome: no video metric reported (qualitative figure only)
direct_conclusion: Temporal consistency, long-horizon drift, occlusion/reappearance and motion fidelity to the source video are claimed or implied but not measured.
author_hypothesis: Treating the style reference as a temporal anchor 'facilitates consistent style propagation' and yields 'temporally coherent results without requiring optical flow guidance'.
confounders: Training data from Ditto is synthesized under depth-consistent conditions; clips with negligible motion were filtered by CLIP frame similarity, so training supervision itself is synthetic.
anchor: this approach yields temporally coherent results without requiring optical flow guidance or test-time optimization

claim: Reuse is via a single LoRA on a specific base model; per-style cost is a forward pass, but the asset is bound to Qwen-Image-Edit-2509 (image) and Wan2.1-1.3B (video), and the video module needs an externally stylized first frame.
experiment: Implementation details: LoRA rank 32 on Qwen-Image-Edit-2509, 4 H100; video model on Wan2.1-1.3B, 8 H100.
measured_outcome: No timing, memory or portability measurements reported.
direct_conclusion: Training-time reuse structure is stated; no inference cost or cross-backbone evidence.
author_hypothesis: Full fine-tuning yielded negligible gains over LoRA (no numbers).
anchor: fine-tuning all parameters of the Qwen-Image MMDiT Wu et al. (2025a) yielded negligible performance gains
